content.title: Creating robust and efficient infrastructure
content.description: Over the past ten years, Sweden has more than doubled infrastructure funding. Despite this, few are satisfied with the current situation. Rail lines are full, queues stretch along the E6 and a lack of integrated corridor planning means bottlenecks are moved rather than resolved.
content.extendedDescription: Meanwhile, the system is not robust enough. The result is weaker Swedish competitiveness. In this morning discussion, we begin the day in Almedalen by exploring how new organisational models and clearer national priorities can increase both delivery speed and efficiency in building and operating Swedish infrastructure. The goal is simple: to meet growing national freight needs and increasing regional commuting. Participating is Linus Eriksson, CEO of Öresundsbron, who works daily with one of the Nordic region's most important infrastructure links between Copenhagen and Malmö. With extensive experience of transport, regional development and international collaboration, he shares his perspectives on what is needed for infrastructure to be robust, efficient and ready for future needs.

content.title: Who should pay for the climate transition – the state or private capital?
content.description: The climate transition requires enormous investment, but businesses and capital markets need long-term ground rules to feel confident investing. What do long-term ground rules actually mean in practice, and how much responsibility can and should politicians take? Who should pay for the transition – the state or private capital?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we channel capital into the transition's most crucial projects despite high initial costs, long lead times and significant risks? This is a central question for both established industry and the next generation of energy, industrial and climate technology companies, where many innovations get stuck between pilot projects and large-scale implementation.
What role should the state play: regulator, investor or financial guarantor? How should banks, pension funds and other long-term investors act when climate targets, energy security and geopolitics set the parameters? And how can we balance technological neutrality, targeted initiatives and the need to scale up quickly?
At a time when the sustainability agenda is being reshaped and the focus is shifting towards resilience and competitiveness, there is a unique opportunity both to prepare Swedish industry for the future and to transform it. We discuss how to remove obstacles and mobilise long-term capital, particularly pension funds, to accelerate the transition.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The future of security policy — what does the next generation of leaders think?
content.description: Security policy is shaped today, but young people will live with its consequences tomorrow. As threats change rapidly, how should we address security, NATO and international cooperation?

We live in a constantly changing world. With new threats, rapid geopolitical shifts and urgent crises, security policy has become one of the defining issues of our time. Sweden now faces the challenge of navigating an uncertain world, and the decisions we make today will shape the world the next generation must live in tomorrow. How do today's choices affect the future? And what do young people think about the decisions being made now?

Utrikespolitiska förbundet (UFS) and Folk och Försvar invite you to an open debate in which political youth organisations can discuss Sweden's security, foreign and defence policy. Together, they will explore how Sweden can best address national security, international cooperation and NATO's role in uncertain times.

The debate is held at Folk och Försvar's arena in Almedalen, a meeting place for dialogue, knowledge exchange and cooperation on Sweden's security.

content.title: Does Swedish politics need more evidence?
content.description: Many knowledge organisations feel that the evidence they produce does not sufficiently inform decision-making in their fields. What is evidence, how does it relate to politics, and what does bringing evidence into political organisations entail?
content.extendedDescription:
Over an afternoon (14.00-16.00), we will examine the concept of evidence in relation to decision-making, governance and implementation in Swedish politics. The two-hour discussion is divided into three parts, with plenty of time for questions and networking between them. The aim is a nuanced dialogue about how more knowledge-driven decision-making can contribute to more precisely targeted, legally sound and effective policy interventions.

In this first discussion, the heads of the EBA and Delmi secretariats meet an investigative journalist to discuss what bringing evidence into political organisations means, why it matters (if it matters), what happens when political decisions are not based on research, the role of the media and how knowledge organisations can communicate knowledge and make it heard. The discussion draws on development aid and migration policy.

14.40-15.10 Between facts and political opinion
15.20-16.00 Is evidence still relevant in politics?

content.title: From pilot to system – how can the state stimulate social investment?
content.description: Many of society's greatest challenges require long-term preventive measures. Yet these are difficult to finance within today's system. Testing and scaling more solutions requires risk-bearing funds repaid only if and when the interventions actually deliver results.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major societal challenges, from mental ill health and youth crime to growing needs in elderly care. We also know that early, preventive measures are often more effective than late interventions. Yet structures enabling such initiatives to be financed and scaled more widely are still missing.
The seminar discusses the state's role in strengthening Sweden's social investment ecosystem. We highlight concrete proposals, including a national knowledge centre inspired by the British Government Outcomes Lab, a government outcomes fund to co-finance results-based initiatives with municipalities and regions, and ways to mobilise more risk-tolerant capital through state actors such as Saminvest.
We also discuss how a national portal for requests for proposals can connect societal challenges, innovative solutions and investment capital more effectively.

Breakfast is served from 08.00.

speakerTitles: Chair of the Committee on the Constitution

content.title: War, crises and climate: is Nordic energy cooperation enough?
content.description: War, energy crises and climate-related disruptions are putting energy systems under pressure. In the Nordic region, energy markets and infrastructure are closely interconnected across borders, and Sweden plays a central role. How can Nordic cooperation strengthen energy security and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy security has become a central issue in an era marked by war, geopolitical uncertainty and recurring energy crises. Cyber and military attacks in recent years have shown how vulnerable energy systems can be – but also how crucial close Nordic cooperation is. For Sweden, a central actor in the Nordic electricity system, this raises questions about how cooperation can develop to strengthen energy security in the region.

Integrated energy markets and shared solutions have given the Nordic region a strong starting point, but how robust is energy cooperation when the energy system comes under pressure?

Nordisk Energiforskning and Nordiska ministerrådet have mapped energy security in the Nordic region in the report Mapping Energy Security in the Nordics. During the event, we discuss what the findings mean for the Nordic region: what are our shared challenges, what opportunities exist – and how can energy cooperation strengthen Nordic energy security and resilience?

content.title: Electricity is hope — what does Ukraine teach us about the importance of a resilient power system?
content.description: Sweden's electricity system is essential to a functioning society, but easily taken for granted. Experience from Ukraine shows what happens when the power system is truly tested, and what is needed for a secure and reliable electricity grid in Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's electricity system is one of our most critical societal functions, but also something we often take for granted. Its reliable operation today is the result of investments made to address previous crises.

In this seminar, we focus on what happens when the electricity system, and particularly the grids, are truly tested. Drawing on Ukraine's experience, where electricity grids have become a direct target in the war, we gain a concrete picture of what resilience means in practice.

Against this background, we discuss what is needed to prepare our electricity supply for today's challenges. In a new normal shaped by climate change and geopolitical uncertainty, the demands on electricity grids are changing fundamentally.

The way forward is clear. Electricity grids are essential to society and business and must now be equipped for a new era.

content.title: Sustainable urban development – creating attractive and resilient cities
content.description: Cities are changing rapidly. Under pressure from climate crises, demographic shifts and new ways of living and working, we are constantly changing. Yet urban development is too often driven by short-term priorities, fragmented responsibilities and project-by-project thinking instead of a clear strategy.
content.extendedDescription:
Today, we understand more than ever how places affect everyday life, economic development and long-term resilience. One principle remains constant: when people are the starting point, long-term value follows. Through our involvement across the value chain, from early development and construction to investment, operations and long-term ownership, we see how holistic, collaborative approaches reduce risks, strengthen resilience and create lasting value for people, cities and investors. This means integrating social, environmental and economic considerations from the outset, coordinating stakeholders around shared goals and managing development from a lifecycle perspective. But how do we create partnerships that add value, reduce risks and generate growth?

Moderator: Henrik Ahnström, Head of Sustainability and Innovation, Skanska Kommersiell Utveckling Norden

content.title: Home first – how can children avoid placement in care?
content.description: More children are being placed in foster families or residential care homes. Placements may be necessary but often have major consequences for children and very high costs for society. Yet experience shows that early, coordinated support can enable more children to grow up with their families.
content.extendedDescription:
How can society improve timely family support so more children can grow up at home with their own families?
The seminar presents Hemma först in Rättviks kommun. Through early, intensive and coordinated support for families in vulnerable circumstances, it aims to enable more children to remain at home and avoid foster or residential care placements.
We examine the model's structure, methods and organisational changes needed for more preventive social services. The seminar also explores the effects of a more family-strengthening approach on children's lives and municipalities' long-term costs.
The initiative is financed through a social outcomes contract, with an external investor enabling the intervention upfront. The municipality repays only if and as agreed results are achieved. This allows important preventive initiatives without the municipality bearing the full financial risk.

content.title: Does AI create a better life for residents – or just an easier working day for the organisation?
content.description: AI is now being introduced into the public sector for analysis, prioritisation and automation. As algorithms influence healthcare, services and interactions with authorities, a central question arises: does AI lead to better lives for residents, or mainly to more efficient organisations?
content.extendedDescription:
Artificial intelligence is changing how the public sector works. AI is already used for analysis, decision support and automation in everything from healthcare to public services and spatial planning.
Development is often driven by the need to make operations more efficient, address resource shortages or perhaps simply try out new technology. At the same time, the technology raises a more fundamental question: for whom is value being created?
Region Jönköpings län uses the working name Esther to personify the resident: the person its services ultimately exist to serve.
Can AI provide better access, faster service and more accurately targeted support for Esther? Or does the technology risk creating distance between Esther and the organisation? The seminar discusses how AI can be developed and used in ways that actually strengthen the resident's perspective, and how the public sector can ensure that technology serves people rather than the other way around.

content.title: Who is responsible for Sweden's resident data?
content.description:
Public-sector digitalisation is moving fast. More and more interactions between residents and public services take place digitally, from applications and decisions to important public information. Large amounts of sensitive data circulate.
Who is responsible for the infrastructure that handles society's resident data?
content.extendedDescription:
This raises a central question: who is responsible for the infrastructure that handles society's resident data?
At a time of growing cyber threats, information influence operations and a more uncertain world, digital trust, transparency and control are becoming increasingly important. The public sector faces a choice: how do we create digital public services that drive innovation while ensuring secure handling of residents' data? The discussion takes a practical and strategic perspective: how municipalities, government agencies and suppliers can work together to build sustainable and secure digital public infrastructure for the long term in Sweden and Europe.
When digital platforms become part of society's basic functions, the issue is no longer just technology, but democracy, responsibility, trust and control.

content.title: Large-scale flexibility and energy storage – think hydropower and pumped storage
content.description: Sweden's electricity needs are expected to rise sharply as electrification gathers pace. At some times we may face a shortage of power, and at others we may have large electricity surpluses. How does this fit together, and how can investments in hydropower and pumped storage help meet future needs?
content.extendedDescription:
The electrification of industry, transport and society is expected to bring rapidly growing electricity demand. At the same time, an electricity system more dependent on weather places greater demands on flexibility, power capacity and system stability.

Hydropower already plays a central role by providing power capacity, flexibility, ancillary services and large-scale energy storage when the electricity system needs them. Meanwhile, opportunities to strengthen hydropower's capabilities further are being explored through upgrades to existing facilities, capacity increases and investments in pumped storage. Several projects are already under way, and some have been completed. Studies show great potential, but also significant challenges.

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies, industry and political representatives to discuss the role hydropower can play in strengthening the capacity balance and flexibility of the electricity system. Which investments are possible, what have we learned so far, and what matters for making further progress?

content.title: Hydropower, aquatic environments and biodiversity – how do we find the right balance?
content.description: The national plan for modern environmental conditions (NAP) aims to improve aquatic environments without unnecessarily weakening hydropower's role in the climate transition, competitiveness and electricity preparedness. How do we balance aquatic environments, hydropower, biodiversity and local interests in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
The national plan for modern environmental conditions (NAP) requires Sweden's hydropower plants to undergo permit reviews to improve river environments and preserve valuable species and habitats. This is a very extensive process expected to take 20 years. At the same time, hydropower is crucial to the green transition, competitiveness and electricity preparedness.

Policymakers have made clear that NAP should be implemented without affecting hydropower's electricity generation, balancing capability and electricity preparedness more than necessary to comply with EU law. But how do we achieve this in practice? How do we weigh energy and climate benefits against natural environments and biodiversity? What do we do when national interests and local needs conflict?

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies, civil society and political representatives to discuss implementing NAP proportionately and sustainably from a socioeconomic perspective, safeguarding both environmental goals and the energy system's needs.

content.title: Electricity preparedness in uncertain times – hydropower as a unique resource
content.description: Energy supply is a central part of total defence. Hydropower has unique capabilities for Sweden's electricity preparedness, but these risk being lost during environmental permitting. How do we ensure that hydropower's preparedness capabilities are developed rather than dismantled?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe's security situation has changed rapidly. Experience from Ukraine shows how vulnerable energy infrastructure is and how crucial robust electricity generation is to society's resilience.

Hydropower accounts for a substantial share of Sweden's electricity generation and has unique capabilities needed during severe disruptions and war. It is dispatchable, has large energy stores in reservoirs and is geographically distributed across the country, often near population centres. Hydropower's contribution to preparedness is often taken for granted and may be jeopardised during permit reviews.
Meanwhile, some preparedness capabilities have been designed out or forgotten because they have not been needed for a long time.

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies and political representatives to discuss hydropower's strategic importance for electricity preparedness and total defence. How can lost capabilities be restored, and how can we ensure important facilities are not eliminated during environmental reviews?

content.title: The missing link: how can more pupils succeed at school?
content.description: Too many pupils leave compulsory school without eligibility for upper secondary education. The consequences are substantial for individuals and society. Despite many initiatives, schools often struggle to provide timely, appropriate support to pupils at risk of falling behind.
content.extendedDescription:
How can schools support pupils when many begin to lose motivation, attendance and achievement? In years four to six, demands on independence and cognitive abilities increase, as does the need for support at home. Pupils who struggle to meet these demands and cannot rely on sufficient support at home often face a gap between school and home.
The intervention presented aims to fill this gap by combining individual mentoring and targeted subject support through tutoring. Mentors work closely with each pupil facing challenges, helping them establish a weekly plan covering studies and leisure and clarifying when parental support is needed.
Targeted tutoring also helps pupils catch up in core subjects. Mullsjö kommun provides a concrete example of a municipality that has adopted the model. The seminar also explores financing the initiative through a social outcomes contract.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Nuclear weapons in space: physics, politics and the future
content.description: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits nuclear weapons in space, but major powers appear to have renewed interest in deploying weapons systems and countermeasures there. Combined with the growing role of private actors in space, this could have far-reaching consequences for humanity.
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to an interdisciplinary panel discussion with nuclear weapons experts from nuclear physics, peace and conflict research, and civil society. The seminar will discuss:

• What is the greatest danger of nuclear weapons in space – how could they affect life on Earth?
• How would a nuclear explosion in space affect satellites and spacecraft?
• How can nuclear weapons in space be detected; can we verify that states do not have them there?
• How is the Outer Space Treaty observed, and what is its future?
• What diplomatic initiatives can Sweden, as a space nation, take to promote compliance with the Outer Space Treaty?

content.title: The cancer strategy in practice: what is needed to meet growing pressure on cancer care?
content.description: Pressure on cancer care is increasing due to demographic change, new care programmes and rapid developments in areas including diagnostics. How has this changed over time, and what does it mean for Swedish cancer care?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar takes the national cancer strategy as its starting point and focuses on translating it into practical action. There are currently substantial regional differences in the quality, availability and outcomes of cancer care, and responsibilities between central government and regions are often perceived as unclear. Accelerating implementation requires shared, measurable goals, sufficient resources and national follow-up that enables comparison and learning. At the seminar, IHE presents a report commissioned by MSD on how demographic changes, national care programmes and rapid medical technology development have increased care volumes and pressure on healthcare. The discussion addresses barriers, policy instruments and how cooperation between decision-makers, professionals, patients, academia and industry can accelerate the adoption of best practice, with equity as its starting point.

content.title: Can a foundation training year ensure access to dentists nationwide?
content.description: Swedish dental care is high quality, but much of the country, particularly the north, lacks staff. Many newly qualified dentists also find the transition from education to clinical work substantial. Could a foundation training year be part of the solution?
content.extendedDescription:
Dental care in Sweden faces challenges affecting skills supply, patient safety and equitable access. Dentists are unevenly distributed geographically, with pronounced shortages in sparsely populated areas and smaller towns. Patients' chances of receiving timely care therefore vary across the country. Many providers also struggle to recruit and retain dentists, reinforcing the imbalance.
The seminar presents the report "Bastjänstgöringsår för tandläkare", produced by Praktikertjänst and Ramboll. Could a foundation training year help address national skills shortages while strengthening new graduates' clinical skills? What would make it attractive to students and employers?
The seminar brings together dental care stakeholders to discuss the report, including outlines of how a foundation training year could be designed.

content.title: When pupils leave school without eligibility – what does it do to their mental health?
content.description: School should prepare young people for the future. But for too many pupils, it has also become the place where anxiety about that future grows. content.extendedDescription: Every year, around 35,000 pupils enter adulthood without a complete upper secondary qualification, largely because of incomplete compulsory school grades and introductory programmes that trap pupils in past educational failures. They enter adult life uncertain about the future and at risk of exclusion from both further education and work. content.title: From obstacle to enabler – the public sector's role in securing future food supplies
content.description: Swedish farmers face economic, climate-related and structural challenges, while playing a central role in food supplies, preparedness and public health. How can the public sector break down silos and proactively contribute to a more resilient food system?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish farmers are in a perfect storm of high costs, low profitability, extreme weather, generational transitions and a growing regulatory burden. At the same time, their role is crucial to the country's food supply, especially in an era marked by geopolitical uncertainty, climate change and public health challenges. The challenges are both systemic and complex.
What role does the public sector need to play in a system-wide transition that secures Sweden's future food supply and overcomes today's fragmented governance?

To explore this, we invite Anna Olofsson, Director General of Jordbruksverket, and Helene Hellmark Knutsson, County Governor of Västerbottens län, to a strategic discussion. We discuss what systems leadership means in practice and what shifts are needed for the public sector to move from silos to collaboration with producers, consumers and other societal actors, thereby strengthening a more resilient, healthy and sustainable food system.

content.title: Sweden is lagging behind: time to introduce advanced practice nurses throughout the care pathway
content.description: The WHO's 2025 report states that advanced practice nurses (AVS) are crucial to strengthening healthcare. The WHO urges all countries to introduce regulations enabling AVS to improve care quality and accessibility. Sweden is lagging behind in this area.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden still lacks national regulation and lags behind many comparable countries. AVS roles are already established in Denmark, Norway and Iceland, with clear education and competence requirements aligned with international standards.

The 2020–2022 pandemic exposed significant shortcomings in Sweden, particularly in municipal healthcare. Several inquiries therefore recommend introducing AVS in municipal healthcare to strengthen medical expertise, improve staffing and skills provision, and ensure care at the right level. Specialist healthcare, which is becoming increasingly advanced, also has substantial needs for expanded expertise. AVS in surgical care have demonstrated good synergies and teamwork, as well as improved quality for patients. Nationella Vårdkompetensrådet also supports introducing AVS to improve continuity and expertise throughout the care pathway, benefiting patients, staff and society. Why, then, is Sweden taking so long?

content.title: The road to equitable cardiovascular care — what must the new plan include?
content.description: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death and create substantial healthcare needs, while regional differences in access and outcomes persist. The government's forthcoming cardiovascular plan must become an effective tool for prevention, care pathways and equitable care nationwide.
content.extendedDescription: The government has tasked Socialstyrelsen with developing a national action plan to prevent and treat cardiovascular diseases. The seminar discusses what the plan needs to include to meet substantial healthcare needs while reducing regional differences. The focus is on a comprehensive approach spanning prevention and early detection, coordinated care pathways, rehabilitation and long-term follow-up through quality registries. The discussion highlights how implementation should be designed to have a real impact: clear targets and indicators, the division of responsibilities between central government and regions, and the policy tools, incentives and funding solutions needed to ensure equitable access and comparable outcomes nationwide.

content.title: The regional airport of the future – what opportunities and challenges?
content.description: What role will regional airports play in the future? New technology and renewable fuels offer opportunities, but challenges are numerous. Where are we today, and what does the journey ahead look like?
content.extendedDescription:

Sveriges Regionala Flygplatser and Grön Flygplats bring together representatives from aircraft manufacturing, fuels and regional airport operations to discuss concrete solutions already within reach: new aviation technology, Swedish-produced renewable fuel and transformed airport operations. content.title: There is chaos in my head — living with mental ill health
content.description: Am I included in society even if I do not produce? Am I allowed space, and who decides how much? Does everyone have equal rights, or do the conditions differ?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to theatre with conversation:
- My everyday life is blank, or black, or full of conflicting impressions. I navigate without a map and usually get lost.
Once I thought I had found my way, because I trusted the wrong person. It did not go well.

My greatest dream is to have a completely ordinary day.

‘Wake up after a good night's sleep, say goodbye to the little ones, go to work and then home to make dinner before everyone's evening activities begin. Then a calm bedtime with happy, contented children before I get some time to myself with my partner.’

This only happens in my dreams. I am alone, afraid and vulnerable. Usually completely at others' mercy. The pain fills my whole body, and worst of all is the shame of being a failure, unwanted and rejected. My thoughts brush against the unmentionable, but hope lingers that there is help for me. Someone who understands and sees me as I am, and makes me visible again. Help me find that, and the courage to accept it. To dare to believe that I, too, am worth it.

content.title: Patient choice in primary care: dismantle or develop?
content.description: Healthcare is intensely debating independent providers' role and the future of patient choice systems. Meanwhile, we see patient choice in primary care leading to better access and strong continuity. How can we develop the current system without reducing patients' access to care?
content.extendedDescription:
Debate about private healthcare providers and patient choice has intensified on both the right and left. Yet criticism rarely concerns the quality of care delivered; instead, it focuses on governance, oversight and politicians' ability to take responsibility for the whole system. Does patient choice risk becoming a scapegoat for problems really arising from system design and follow-up?
In this seminar, Praktikertjänst presents a new report on the Act on System of Choice in primary care and brings together politicians, care providers and healthcare professionals for a nuanced discussion of future healthcare. Drawing on practical regional experience, we discuss how LOV can evolve to secure freedom of choice while strengthening access, continuity and quality. The aim is to contribute to reforms combining innovation and long-term trust.

content.title: Hemp for sustainable construction and increased carbon storage
content.description: Hemp can support more environmentally sound buildings and a sustainable bio-based economy. By making greater use of hemp again, with modern construction as its main market, we can radically reduce CO2 emissions.
content.extendedDescription: Hemp is a plant that people around the world have used for thousands of years. It is also an efficient carbon sink with industrial potential. Its many uses include shipping, agriculture, paper, printing, pharmaceuticals, food and construction. Hemp can radically reduce CO2 emissions by reducing the use of lime and cement, store CO2 in biomass, provide good insulation and make use of materials' hygroscopic properties to regulate the indoor climate naturally. Examples of buildings insulated with hemp include multi-storey housing for low-income residents in Paris, an environmentally adapted Marks & Spencers in England, municipal buildings in the Netherlands, Åhléns' main warehouse in Sweden and half-timbered houses among Visby's historic buildings. Hemp can help us build a more robust society: a local bio-based economy that supplies materials for homes and products while forming a logical part of an ecological cycle.

content.title: The transition that matters: how can we give new nurses a stronger start in their careers?
content.description: Healthcare faces a global shortage of nurses, making the transition from education to working life particularly important. Around 20% of newly qualified nurses in Sweden consider leaving the profession early, during their first four years, and stress is a major reason.
content.extendedDescription: Many new nurses feel highly engaged at first, but can sometimes lose that engagement because of high demands, a lack of support and stress. A supportive working environment with clear leadership, reasonable staffing levels, positive peer support and well-designed induction programmes helps new nurses grow into their professional roles. These organisational conditions increase job satisfaction and contribute to better health, lower stress, higher-quality care and less sickness absence. Research also shows that socialisation programmes and brief stress-prevention interventions effectively reduce ill health among prospective and newly employed nurses, highlighting the importance of integrating evidence-based support into the transition to clinical work. Organisations that succeed in creating such environments also often have lower sickness absence and more engaged staff and nurses.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Member of the Riksdag's Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Metal and mineral supply in a changing world
content.description: Metal and mineral supply is affected by a changing world. New regulations, changing market conditions and shifting risks create new circumstances for society and industry. How can stakeholders be mobilised and research and innovation initiatives launched to respond?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has substantial mineral resources, strong industrial expertise and favourable conditions for contributing to a sustainable supply of metals and minerals. At the same time, the world around us is changing rapidly. New and stricter regulations, increased information and traceability requirements, changing market conditions and an evolving risk landscape affect developments throughout the value chain.

In this context, Swedish Metals & Minerals brings together stakeholders, identifies needs and initiates research and innovation efforts that respond to new challenges and opportunities. The seminar starts from how the programme operates in a changing world and highlights examples of initiatives that strengthen the ability to act as conditions change.
The programme and speakers will be updated.

content.title: Lifelong learning and skills shortages – how do we make them fit together?
content.description: Matching problems in Sweden's labour market are substantial, while the need for lifelong learning is growing. For more people to retrain, pursue further education and enter employment, better support is needed to understand occupations, education and labour market needs.
content.extendedDescription: More educational opportunities alone are not enough to make lifelong learning work in practice. People also need better support to understand emerging occupations, the skills in demand and which routes actually lead to work. This discussion brings together perspectives on skills provision from the labour market, education, civil society and young people. We discuss how to strengthen connections between individual development, educational provision and employers' needs. Where are today's gaps, and what is needed to make career transitions, further education and entry into employment possible for more people? The aim is to highlight a growing societal challenge and open a discussion about building better bridges between people, education and jobs.

content.title: How do we ensure the right pharmaceutical expertise when systems are tested by crisis and war?
content.description: Crises, war and heightened geopolitical tensions put pressure on the pharmaceutical system. How do we ensure the expertise needed to strengthen preparedness and medicine supplies? What coordination, specialist knowledge and training are required throughout the chain to withstand the next crisis?
content.extendedDescription:
Crises, geopolitical change, war near Europe's borders and recurring shortages place intense pressure on the pharmaceutical system. Sweden's pharmaceutical expertise needs to be recognised more clearly as a resource for strengthening preparedness and medicine supplies. The discussion examines future education and skills needs: how should preparedness work be designed and coordinated? What roles will pharmacists with different qualifications play in crisis and war, and are new skills needed? How can these perspectives be developed in initial, continuing and further education, and how can lifelong learning prepare professionals for changing conditions?

Representatives of academia, pharmacies, regions, authorities, total defence, politics and industry discuss in an open roundtable what is needed for Sweden to be better prepared for future pharmaceutical challenges.

content.title: The EU's forthcoming renovation requirements — a goldmine or a climate disaster?
content.description: The EU's forthcoming renovation requirements put Sweden at a crossroads: will the renovation wave become an engine of circular innovation, or will we remain stuck in linear working methods that make the transition more expensive, slower and less sustainable?
content.extendedDescription: The EU's new Energy Performance of Buildings Directive is driving a massive transformation of Europe's building stock. Sweden, with hundreds of thousands of buildings requiring energy-efficiency improvements before 2050, faces one of its largest renovation waves ever. Yet linear working methods, complicated rules and a lack of clear incentives risk holding back the circular innovation Europe is now pursuing. Requirements for minimum standards, lifecycle calculations and renovation plans present both opportunity and risk: either we take the lead in smart energy efficiency and circular systems, or we fall behind while other countries already view their buildings as valuable material banks. This seminar brings together experts and decision-makers to discuss whether Sweden is ready for the shift and what is needed to prevent politics, industry and regulations becoming the bottleneck.

content.title: Bakers and welders, the same question: how do we secure the future skills supply?
content.description: Skills supply is one of society's major challenges today. Intensive efforts are being made everywhere to attract new employees, yet challenges persist. Why have we not made more progress?
content.extendedDescription:
Skills supply challenges affect not only day-to-day operations but also the ability to grow, develop and meet future needs. Despite major efforts to attract workers such as bakers, pastry chefs and welders, difficulties remain in encouraging more people to choose relevant courses and careers, and in some cases even ensuring that the right training is available.

In this presentation, Sveriges bagare & konditorer and Svetskommissionen share their experiences of skills challenges in their sectors. With different circumstances but similar needs and challenges, they raise questions about attractiveness, recruitment barriers and the link between education and working life.

The aim is to highlight where the challenges are greatest and open a discussion about the perspectives, partnerships and possible ways forward that politics, education and business need to consider.

content.title: Equality before the law and self-determination are fundamental human rights – do they apply to everyone?
content.description: How does self-determination work in practice for people with multiple and intellectual disabilities? What is needed for people requiring decision-making support to have their wishes respected instead of facing questioning, exclusion and discrimination?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from self-determination as a human rights issue. Article 12 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities establishes the right to recognition as a person before the law, to exercise legal capacity equally with others, and to receive the support needed to exercise this right.

We highlight the gap between rights and reality for people with multiple and intellectual disabilities who need support to interpret and express their wishes.
The Jag bestämmer project examines how supported decision-making works, but also why people's wishes are often questioned or disregarded by authorities, other organisations and those around them. Insufficient knowledge and negative attitudes risk leading to exclusion and IQ-based discrimination. We begin with the project's preliminary findings, then discuss the issue with a knowledgeable panel.

Jag bestämmer is an Arvsfonden project in cooperation with RFS, FUB, Hjärnkraft and Autism Sverige.

content.title: Scaling up a greener food system – who will do the work?
content.description: Everyone is talking about scaling up a greener food chain. But who will do the work? Today, there is a large gap between ambitions, education and skills. This gap risks becoming a major challenge not only for the industries concerned, but for Swedish society as a whole and our food supply.
content.extendedDescription:
Green expansion has become a key phrase in discussions of Swedish food production, preparedness and transition. Fundamentally, it means increasing production, strengthening competitiveness and simultaneously meeting higher demands for sustainability and climate responsibility. But one question risks being overlooked: who will do the work?

As LRF and Livsmedelsföretagen share their perspectives, the focus turns to a growing gap between political ambitions, the education system's capacity and the industries' actual skills needs. If more people do not see the sector as a possible future, and if routes into education and employment remain unclear or non-existent, green expansion risks slowing before it has even gathered pace. Improved opportunities for adult education are crucial.

This presentation and the debate that follows therefore highlight a question both politicians and businesses must address: what conditions must be strengthened now to make the transition possible in practice?

content.title: We face major climate change – how can we plan and build a sustainable society?
content.description: The transition concerns both concrete measures to reduce emissions from different sectors of society and the lifestyle changes needed to achieve the goal of limiting the planet's temperature increase to 1.5–2 degrees.
content.extendedDescription: We must reduce greenhouse gas emissions and stay within planetary boundaries. Fossil fuels must be replaced with renewable energy sources. Ecological sustainability means shifting agriculture, forestry and marine production to regenerative methods that preserve biodiversity. Social sustainability means a society that meets people's basic needs and gives them meaning in life. Cities must be transformed to rely on walking, cycling and public transport rather than mass car use. Existing buildings and new developments must become energy-efficient, and the materials used must not cause large climate emissions. We must move away from today's throwaway consumption towards quality, repairability and reuse. Production must therefore shift from a linear to a circular economy. Economic sustainability means moving away from a society based on growth, reducing economic inequality and making these changes possible.

content.title: What responsibility do employers have for sexual harassment?
content.description: Surveys show that more than 150 000 people each year report experiencing sexual harassment at work. Despite legislation and other measures, the problem persists. Why are employers failing to stop and prevent sexual harassment in the workplace?
content.extendedDescription:
Sexual harassment in working life is well known and clearly documented. Employees experience harassment and sexual harassment from managers and colleagues, as well as people who do not work at the same workplace, known as third parties. Women under 30 are the most exposed.

#MeToo clearly showed that employers do not do enough to prevent sexual harassment and often fail to take adequate action.

DO's panel discusses what employers can do to prevent and stop sexual harassment and what the statutory duty to investigate and take action actually means.

content.title: Everyone talks about prevention – why is it not happening in practice?
content.description: Schools have a clear duty to work preventively, from mental health and fundamental values to ANDTS (alcohol, drugs, doping, tobacco and gambling) and safety. Yet research, public-agency reports and surveys show that prevention is often squeezed out of schools' daily work.
content.extendedDescription:
Several reports from Skolinspektionen and Skolverket show shortcomings in schools' preventive work relating to safety, a calm learning environment and degrading treatment.
Current ANDTS data from school professionals confirms this. In a new survey, 80 per cent say schools do not do enough prevention, while 76 per cent say pupils rarely or never get to discuss alcohol in lessons. Many also identify concrete barriers: 68 per cent cite a lack of time and 64 per cent a lack of materials.
This reveals a clear pattern: the willingness is there, but the conditions are not.
The seminar discusses why preventive work, which everyone agrees is crucial, still struggles to have an impact in practice, and what is needed to strengthen it.

Sample questions:

Why does prevention have insufficient impact in schools' daily work?
Which conditions are currently missing?
What is needed to move from ambition to practice?

content.description: How do we help young people make well-informed choices about their futures amid uncertainty, wrong turns and skills shortages?

content.title: Can properties become Sweden's next preparedness resource by relieving an electricity system under pressure?
content.description: Sweden's electricity system is under pressure from power shortages, weather and increasing demands. Can properties become an active resource that reduces peaks, stores energy and strengthens preparedness? What opportunities and barriers exist, and what is needed to unlock buildings' hidden potential?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's electricity system faces growing pressures, from power shortages and electrification to extreme weather and a greater security focus. Yet an often overlooked resource lies within our communities: buildings. Smarter controls, energy storage, reduced power demand and integration with local energy systems can enable buildings to relieve the grid when it is under greatest strain. Despite this potential, unclear regulations, weak incentives and ambiguous responsibilities are slowing progress. This seminar explores how properties can become part of Sweden's next preparedness resource, which technical and political barriers must be removed, and how industry, public authorities and decision-makers can cooperate to build a more resilient energy system. The question is no longer whether the need exists, but how quickly we dare to think differently.

content.title: How well equipped are schools to support children and young people in crisis and grief?
content.description: Every year, thousands of children and young people experience crises, grief and difficult life events. For many, school becomes the most important place for security, structure and a functioning everyday life. Yet many schools lack the support, knowledge and conditions to help them.
content.extendedDescription:
Schools can make a decisive difference for children experiencing crisis and grief and prevent future mental ill health if they have the knowledge and conditions needed. But what is the reality today?

How do you talk about what has happened?
How do you support the child – and the class?
How do you engage with relatives and other adults?
And how do staff look after one another when the difficult situation affects them too?

When crisis and grief affect a child, they also affect the school. Support needs to be equitable across the country so that neither schools nor children are left alone in difficult situations. With support from Folkhälsomyndigheten, Ericastiftelsen has developed initiatives to strengthen schools' preparedness and expertise in crisis support and suicide prevention.

The seminar discusses what schools need to support children experiencing crisis and grief, both immediately and in the longer term. And what is needed to prevent children and young people from falling through the cracks when life becomes difficult.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for the climate during refurbishment?
content.description: Tenant fit-outs and interior refurbishments are a recurring but often overlooked source of climate impact. There is considerable potential to reduce the carbon footprint through reuse, clear incentives and better evidence for decisions. How can we seize this opportunity?
content.extendedDescription:
A large part of the climate impact of the construction and property sector arises from recurring refurbishments of premises. This also presents a concrete opportunity to reduce the carbon footprint by working more systematically with reuse, long service life and climate data for interiors. HI-märkningen, Sweden's first environmental certification for premises, developed with RISE and around thirty organisations, provides a framework for setting requirements during interior design and refurbishment. Clear criteria and independent verification enable tenants, property owners and designers to reduce climate impact where decisions are actually made.
The work is now being developed further through the project “Cirkulär kontorsutveckling börjar hos hyresgästen”, focusing on generic climate data for interior products and how incentives can be changed from the earliest stages. The discussion explores how these tools can contribute to a more circular and climate-conscious construction sector.

content.title: National cancer strategy — together we can move from words to action
content.description: Cancer is the leading cause of years of life lost in Sweden. But healthcare has made major progress, and mortality in Sweden is now among the lowest in the EU, partly thanks to the national cancer strategy that has guided the way. The government has updated the strategy to meet future needs.
content.extendedDescription:
The cancer strategy aims to reduce cancer risk, improve early detection, increase survival and provide the best possible quality of life during and after illness. It also emphasises the need for greater cooperation across organisations and sectors. Samverkansgruppen för svensk cancervård has been formed to coordinate this work.

Cancer care in Sweden is developing rapidly, with work under way in every area identified in the updated strategy. The strategy now provides a unifying force and a new opportunity to set priorities together. In Almedalen, we in Samverkansgruppen för svensk cancervård invite you to discuss how to move from words to action. What is the highest priority? Which partnerships need strengthening? What do the regions need from us to deliver world-class cancer care?

content.title: The lottery for people with lung disease – which postcode wins access to adequate care and new technology?
content.description: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is a stigmatised condition affecting hundreds of thousands of Swedes. Despite new medical innovations, access to these technologies varies widely. Standardised care pathways ensuring equitable, evidence-based care are lacking.
content.extendedDescription:
COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is a stigmatised condition affecting hundreds of thousands of Swedes. Although new medical innovations improve quality of life and reduce patients' need for healthcare visits, access to these technologies varies considerably across our 21 regions. At the same time, standardised care pathways are lacking, despite being an important component in ensuring equitable, evidence-based care for people living with COPD, regardless of where in the country they live. This challenge requires strategic collaboration and fresh thinking.

How can we ensure that everyone living with lung disease, regardless of background or place of residence, has equitable access to the best possible treatment?

During the debate, we bring together healthcare decision-makers and stakeholders, politicians and companies to highlight challenges and opportunities associated with introducing innovative technology and national care pathways in COPD care.

content.title: Stop wasting – make the most of what we already have
content.description: The construction and transport sectors currently account for around half of Sweden's climate emissions and consume significant financial and material resources.
content.extendedDescription:
The construction and transport sectors currently account for around half of Sweden's climate emissions and consume significant financial and material resources. But Sweden can become a world leader in resource-efficient development of the built environment with a low climate footprint if we move from resource-intensive new construction projects to circular business models that create value in what already exists. This requires us to stop measuring success solely in new construction or kilometres of newly laid asphalt, and instead focus on meeting needs and providing accessibility.

We highlight concrete examples of solutions and present work to transform Sweden's built environment sector. A warm welcome to the presentation and discussion!

content.title: What would a secure and cost-effective future energy supply in Sweden look like?
content.description: How much energy will we use in the short and long term? How can Sweden secure its energy supply? What do new EU requirements mean for energy supply? How can it be made robust enough to provide essential energy services even during extreme weather, sabotage or war?
content.extendedDescription: Over recent decades, forecasts of future energy use have proved exaggerated. The government now says electricity use should double by 2050, regardless of electricity costs. This is unlikely to happen, but unclear or incorrect forecasts can lead to misguided investment. What is a reasonable long-term level? How far will new EU requirements on energy conservation and climate adaptation take us, and what difficulties arise in implementing them? What limits exist for future electricity production from nuclear and wind power? Global uncertainty affects fuel availability and prices, alongside increased opportunities to sabotage energy supply, drone weapons and extreme weather. Could local systems maintain electricity supply during temporary or prolonged outages?

content.title: Society under pressure – how do we step up defence capabilities?
content.description: The security situation is more uncertain than it has been for a long time. Wars are ongoing, partnerships are being tested and new risks are emerging. What does Sweden need to act quickly, strengthen preparedness and meet threats in an increasingly unpredictable world?

Institutions and partnerships that have provided guarantees for many years are being tested, including the NATO and UN systems. content.title: What do you know about species extinction?
content.description: Biodiversity is central to balanced ecosystems and resilience to climate change. But we are losing biodiversity at a rate 1,000 times faster than during any previous mass extinction in Earth's 4.5-billion-year history. How can we address this crisis?
content.extendedDescription:
Biodiversity can seem like an abstract concept: perhaps something that brings pandas or rainforests to mind, or EU legislation affecting Swedish forestry. But what does it actually mean to talk about the "Holocene extinction" and "biodiversity loss"?

To make this existential issue tangible, Fältbiologerna is organising an interactive quiz: "What do you know about dead animals?" Our young experts will do more than preach about creeping lady's-tresses or the three-toed woodpecker. We ask the audience questions about species on the new Swedish Red List and ask them to explain exactly why these species are threatened with extinction. Which human activities drive species extinction? What can we do about it? And what kind of planet are our decision-makers leaving to the youngest generations?

Does this sound like something for you? Test your knowledge and discover what you really know about dead animals.

content.title: From requirements to capability — how do we build robust municipal preparedness?
content.description: New requirements for municipalities' and regions' preparedness for crisis and war are about to become reality, but how should they be translated into operational capability? content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's municipalities and regions face stricter requirements for preparedness for crisis and war. The inquiry behind LKRB has now been followed by a bill to parliament, with municipal operational capability at its centre.

But how are these requirements put into practice?

Building robust preparedness involves more than planning. It requires effective leadership, cooperation, technical systems and practical capability even when normal structures come under pressure.

The seminar explores these questions and how operational preparedness can be built in municipalities, as well as the roles that central government, municipalities, business and civil society can play in developing robust, sustained preparedness. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.

content.title: A climate-friendly, secure and affordable energy supply in Sweden
content.description: Energy supplies must be secure, have a low climate impact and be affordable. This means the electricity grid must be well developed, energy storage must be available to cope with power outages, and combustion must largely be replaced by electric motors and heat pumps. What might such a scenario look like?
content.extendedDescription:
Electricity use in Sweden has remained more or less unchanged for several decades, despite GDP more than doubling and the population increasing by over 25%. Meanwhile, electricity production has risen steadily over the past 15 years. So far, demand for increased electricity use has been met through savings and efficiency improvements. The green transition is expected to require a great deal of new electricity, but electricity demand cannot keep rising indefinitely.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of solar power, wind power, bioenergy and nuclear power? What psychological and physical limits exist for new electricity generation, and what margins need to be left for the future?
What would the situation look like if, instead of focusing all our thinking on new production, we invested heavily in energy efficiency and replaced as much combustion as possible with electric motors and heat pumps? According to calculations I will present, this would considerably reduce energy needs and greatly cut greenhouse gas emissions.

content.title: Icebreakers from a Nordic perspective: do total defence and the Arctic require new thinking on functions and technology?

Geopolitics encompasses security, security of supply, strategic polar research and icebreakers.

content.title: Turning headwinds into business value: success factors for profitable electrification of heavy vehicles
content.description: Some argue that the energy transition's next major leap, electrifying public transport, boats, buses, machinery and heavy vehicles, has stalled. The pace has slowed alongside declining demand and profitability. Sometimes, the claim is that there is no business case.
content.extendedDescription:
Progress has been slower than the optimistic forecasts that dominated a few years ago. But is it premature to dismiss business models for electrifying heavy transport? Several Swedish stakeholders demonstrate the opposite.

Both private and public sectors offer examples where electric fleets provide a competitive advantage and business value. How did they achieve this? What are the success factors? Which obstacles have they encountered and overcome? And what role has policy played? The seminar examines developments from different angles and highlights key factors for overcoming barriers and daring to invest. Is it mainly about grid expansion, access to electricity and power capacity, technical solutions such as battery development and charging infrastructure, or economic viability through reasonable investment conditions, financing and business models and adapted electricity tariffs to stimulate demand? What political ground rules and policy instruments are needed?

content.title: With AI, we can analyse, manage and follow up requirements
content.description: Construction projects set requirements for execution, technology, materials and sustainability. When projects move into production, the link to the original requirements is often broken. How can AI support the management and follow-up of requirements and contribute to circularity in construction, from design and building to property management?
content.extendedDescription:
Construction projects set extensive contractual and sustainability requirements. These are incorporated into technical specifications and procurement, but when the project moves into production, the link to the original requirements is often broken. Follow-up becomes difficult and traceability is lost.
Can AI help the construction sector follow up requirements throughout a building's life cycle?
Over the past year, we have developed and tested AI assistants for requirements management that can identify, structure and follow up requirements throughout the construction and property management process, from the brief and design stages to production and management.
At the seminar, we demonstrate how AI is now being used in several related areas:
• AI assistant for requirements management
• AI guide for circular offerings
• AI guide for ESG
• Maturity model for digital sustainability management
We discuss how digital structure and AI can contribute to more effective management and follow-up of requirements and more circular processes in construction.

content.title: When AI passes the exam: who takes responsibility for patient safety?
content.description: AI and advanced technology challenge today's assessments. How do we ensure legally sound exams that assess the student, rather than AI or unauthorised aids? What is at stake for trust in academic degrees? Is patient safety at risk?
content.extendedDescription:
When AI can write essays, solve exam questions and imitate students' language, one of universities' foundations, legally sound assessment, becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. What happens when technology outpaces regulations, and how does this affect professions in which inadequate knowledge can endanger patient safety?

The seminar begins by presenting the government assignment ‘Mapping measures against cheating in distance learning’, followed by a panel debate. What is needed to ensure legally sound assessment when generative AI makes cheating easy, even in invigilated exams where legal restrictions limit checks? Can these challenges be met?

Participants explore legal, academic, regulatory, student and teacher perspectives, alongside healthcare's perspective, where inadequate knowledge can have particularly serious consequences.

content.title: Could unfired clay become a key material in future climate-smart construction?
content.description: The construction sector is looking for materials with low climate and environmental impacts and good indoor environmental properties. Unfired clay is one of the world's oldest building materials, but modern standardisation and industrially manufactured products are now generating renewed interest.
content.extendedDescription:
Unfired clay has been used in buildings for thousands of years, but has long been uncommon in modern construction. In recent years, standardisation, including SIS standards, and factory-made products adapted to today's building systems have brought renewed interest in the material.
The seminar explores how unfired clay can be used in modern construction, for example in plaster, mortar, blocks and finished surfaces.
We discuss the material's properties and the functions it can provide in buildings. Because the clay does not need to be fired at high temperatures, it has a low climate impact. Clay can also help regulate moisture and temperature in buildings and provide moisture and fire protection for bio-based structures.
The seminar also considers how clay-based finishes and coloured clay plasters can serve as alternatives to conventional interior finishes, and how demountable wall systems can be built using clay.

content.title: What does it cost when children stop reading — in knowledge, independence and confidence in the future?
content.description: Reading builds language, knowledge and the ability to find one's way in a complex world. But what happens to schools, working life and democracy if we cease to be a nation of readers — and what is needed to reverse the trend?

In this seminar, we explore how reading builds language, subject knowledge and critical thinking, while also strengthening independence, judgement and the ability to navigate a complex world. When more people read, opportunities for participation and community increase, and it becomes easier to resist disinformation and polarisation.
We discuss the responsibility different parts of society have to safeguard reading as a foundation for democracy and confidence in the future, and what actually works when we want to reverse the trend.

The seminar takes the form of a discussion between researchers, practitioners and voices from schools.

content.title: When support and assessment do not align – how can we secure pupils' right to digital tools?
content.description: Pupils who need digital tools to support learning must be allowed to use them when their knowledge is assessed. As schools undergo reform, a crucial question is how to ensure equity means the right conditions for each pupil rather than identical conditions for everyone. What is needed for an accessible school system?
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a panel discussion bringing together perspectives on one of schools' most central questions: ensuring every pupil has the conditions to reach their full potential. Starting from concrete examples of everyday school life, the discussion highlights challenges when access to support varies. Equity means giving every pupil precisely the support they need to succeed.
The panel includes Idor Svensson, Professor of Clinical Psychology at Linnéuniversitetet, with extensive experience researching dyslexia. His perspective deepens understanding of how the right tools affect learning and participation. Eva Lundin, an educator at Solbergaskolan in Visby, also participates, bringing a close classroom perspective and experience of using digital services to create accessibility in practice. By bringing research and practice together, the seminar aims to drive a solution-oriented discussion about tomorrow's schools.

content.title: Can Sweden avoid the multibillion bill for plastic?
content.description: Sweden pays large sums to the EU because we are not meeting plastic packaging recycling targets. What is needed to reverse the trend? Which measures effectively increase recycling?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden pays billions in penalties to the EU because we fail to recycle plastic. Responsibility is spread across producers' design choices, household sorting, municipal collection, recycling facilities and buyers of recycled materials.

The EU is now tightening the rules. Sweden is introducing new waste legislation. Increasing recycling is about reducing climate emissions and making the EU more self-sufficient. How do we move from paying for failure to building a profitable circular economy? How do we reach the target of recycling 55 per cent of plastic packaging?

Recycling organisation Näringslivets Producentansvar (NPA) invites you to a discussion of the political decisions needed to turn a cost into a resource.

Please arrive early enough to have breakfast before the discussion begins.

content.title: Mental Health and Human Sustainability in Defense Systems
content.description: War places immense psychological pressure on those serving on the frontline and across defense systems. Mental health and recovery are essential for sustaining defense capacity and societal resilience. How can resilience become part of national security and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
This event expands the discussion by bringing practical experience from Ukraine, where the psychological impact of prolonged war on those serving on the frontline has become a critical challenge for defense systems and society.

Repower’s work is based on an innovative recovery approach developed through programs supporting frontline medical personnel exposed to the psychological pressure of war. The approach combines recovery, peer exchange and holistic practices aimed at restoring human capacity and long-term resilience.

This space creates a discussion on how mental health can be integrated into defense and preparedness strategies. Participants will reflect on resilience as a factor of national security.

It takes place in a curated space where art serves as a communication tool. A thought-provoking installation translates invisible psychological pressure into a tangible public experience and opens space for dialogue across defense, policy and civil society perspectives.

content.title: Can circular solutions address water shortages?
content.description: The availability of freshwater is declining worldwide as global warming progresses. This is also happening on Öland, Gotland and in south-eastern Sweden. At the same time, rainfall is becoming more frequent, with heavy rain falling over shorter periods – rain that causes damage and usually cannot be captured.
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, demand for water in agriculture, industry and society is increasing. A traditional way of addressing this is to produce drinking water from seawater. We want to highlight other solutions to this problem and a change in outlook and ambition: from “clean enough to discharge” to “as circular as possible”. Recovering resources already present in our processes and systems reduces the need to keep producing new ones. This applies particularly to rain that falls and quickly drains into the sea through drainage ditches, but also to wastewater from municipal treatment plants and industry. Circular solutions enable not only water but also input materials to be returned to the circular loop.
The seminar examines water-related challenges and solutions tested at full scale, and highlights industry's ability to lead the implementation of circular solutions.

Introduction by Anders Hagfeldt, Vice-Chancellor of Uppsala universitet.

content.title: Source to Sea and the Catchment Approach – voices from around the Baltic Sea
content.description: Scaling up Swedish measures and implementing the EU Water Framework Directive can cut nutrient emissions to the Baltic Sea and restore freshwater ecosystems. But progress is too slow—what can Sweden learn from neighbouring countries’ source‑to‑sea projects?
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea's ecosystems are threatened by eutrophication, environmental toxins and many freshwater and coastal ecosystems in the catchment area have been destroyed by physical impacts. 
A number of large national projects focusing on scaling up action work and implementing the EU's Water Framework Directive and reducing the impact on the Baltic Sea have been started in our neighboring countries. In the seminar, experts from Finland and Estonia together with Swedish experts will reflect on and discuss the following questions:
- Which strategies and approaches are successful for scaling up the remediation work? 
- What are the challenges to succeed in scaling up action on a national level?
- How do we organize learning and exchange of experience between the Baltic Sea countries?
- What are the next steps for the Swedish work protecting and restoring the Baltic Sea?

content.title: From knowledge to action – what is needed to reduce nutrient losses from agriculture?
content.description: Agriculture around the Baltic Sea is the single largest source of phosphorus and nitrogen emissions into lakes and seas. We know which measures effectively reduce these losses into our sensitive sea, but what prevents farmers from implementing them?
content.extendedDescription:
Agriculture around the Baltic Sea is the single largest source of phosphorus and nitrogen emissions into the sea, contributing to eutrophication, algal blooms and oxygen depletion in one of the world's most sensitive inland seas. Extensive knowledge exists today about measures that effectively reduce nutrient losses from farmland, including improved nutrient balances, catch crops, structural liming, gypsum treatment, buffer strips and adapted tillage. Yet the transition is slower than environmental targets and the ecosystem require. What actually determines whether measures are implemented? Is it economics, motivation, regulations, knowledge transfer, production risks or something else?

During this panel discussion, farmers from different parts of the Baltic Sea region share their experiences of actively reducing nutrient losses. Experts then discuss barriers and opportunities for encouraging more people to take action for a cleaner sea.

content.title: Can waste collection close to homes be both simple and efficient?
content.description: Waste collection close to homes is an issue that engages people. Space is tight in cities, while distances are long in rural areas. Yet some municipalities combine high collection rates with satisfied residents. What is the key to successful collection?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's waste collection landscape is being redrawn. Responsibility for collecting your packaging has shifted from producers to municipalities. A race against time is now under way to ensure that collection also takes place close to homes by 2027.

The question is: will the new system increase collection? To meet recycling targets, Sweden must collect twice as much plastic. And will it be efficient enough? Collection is a hidden cost on your supermarket receipt. Without a smart nationwide system, we all pay the price.

The seminar takes stock of progress with collection close to homes. What is working well? How do municipal waste companies and property owners resolve challenging cases? What can municipalities learn from one another?

Recycling organisation Näringslivets Producentansvar (NPA) invites you to a discussion on the role of collection in the circular economy.

content.title: 50 years of workplace conflict: what does the employment law expert know that the rest of us miss?
content.description: Workplace conflicts are rarely just about laws; they are about leadership, responsibility and people. What can we learn from 50 years of employment disputes and working environment issues? What patterns recur when the rules of working life meet reality?
content.extendedDescription:
For five decades, Tommy Iseskog has been one of Sweden's most influential experts on employment law and the working environment. His books, analyses and training have helped generations of managers, lawyers and HR specialists understand the rules of working life. But behind the expert role is also a personal story.

How do views of responsibility, conflict and justice change after a lifetime spent dealing with the most complex workplace issues? What really happens in organisations when laws meet reality? And what has Tommy Iseskog learned after writing no fewer than 300 books, some of them novels?

We meet Tommy Iseskog in an open and personal conversation about working life, writing and the people behind the legal provisions.
It will be a fascinating story in which law meets life experience, sharp analysis blends with storytelling, and the audience meets the person behind one of the best-known voices in working life.

content.title: When Civil Society Becomes Part of a Nation’s Defence System
content.description: In Ukraine, civil society has become an operational part of the defence ecosystem. How do civic initiatives, volunteer networks and recovery programs strengthen resilience and support those serving on the frontline?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine’s war has revealed how civil society can become an operational component of a nation’s defence system. Volunteer networks, civic initiatives and independent organizations play a critical role in supporting those serving on the frontline, often responding faster and more flexibly than traditional structures.

Repower’s recovery programs supporting frontline medics demonstrate how civil initiatives can strengthen the human dimension of defence by addressing psychological resilience and recovery after extreme stress.

The discussion explores how these models of civil engagement interact with formal defence structures and how they contribute to national resilience. The conversation also connects Ukraine’s experience with the Nordic perspective, including Sweden’s Total Defence doctrine and the role of civil society organizations in crisis preparedness. It invites reflection on how cooperation between state and civic initiatives can strengthen future security systems.
