content.title: Prioritising migraine – an opportunity for Swedish growth
content.description: Migraine is a common neurological disease and the most disabling disease among people of working age. Beyond considerable personal suffering, it places major strains on private life, employers and society as a whole. Solutions exist for equitable, effective and individualised migraine care.
content.extendedDescription:
Around 1.4 million Swedes suffer from migraine of varying severity. Despite effective treatments and care guidelines, migraine is underdiagnosed, undertreated and underprioritised in Swedish healthcare. Who takes responsibility for those without a diagnosis, those not receiving the care they need and those forced to self-medicate?
We will present a new compilation of data on the societal burden and consequences for the public and private sectors.
The remaining question is who will take responsibility and show the way towards equitable, effective and individualised migraine care that creates value for us all. That is what we will discuss.

content.title: A well-treated patient: are data lakes and follow-up the keys to the right individual treatment?
content.description: Despite major investment in healthcare and innovative treatments, the desired results are not always achieved. Many patients do not receive the follow-up and evaluation needed for treatment to remain effective throughout. The potential of data-driven approaches and cooperation between healthcare services and patients often goes untapped.
content.extendedDescription:
How do we create future healthcare in which more people meet treatment goals, measured both by patient-reported outcome measures (PROM) and objective disease parameters, so that individuals and society gain the greatest possible benefit? Could the key be systematically recording and following up treatment outcomes, with smart data collection and use in close cooperation between patients and healthcare services creating the conditions for better long-term care and health, while giving healthcare services greater opportunities to optimise organisation, working methods and resource use?

The discussion also aims to highlight how innovation in healthcare and life sciences drives progress for the benefit of patients, care quality and society's long-term sustainability.

This event is part of Life Science Day, an initiative of the Medicon Village research park.

content.title: Important measures for a healthier Baltic Sea
content.description: The Baltic Sea is one of the world's most polluted and overfished seas, but the right measures can reduce eutrophication, strengthen biodiversity and address climate change while enabling people to use the sea and its resources.
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea is a unique and sensitive ecosystem that has long faced major pressures, from overfishing to pollution, eutrophication and coastal development. Climate change is now adding further pressure. There are therefore calls for better protection and restoration of the marine environment.
At the same time, there is strong pressure to increase use of the sea for shipping, aquaculture, tourism, defence and wind power. Can these different ambitions be reconciled?

Fortunately, history shows that when people around the Baltic Sea come together and make wise decisions, major improvements and benefits can be achieved. Much has been done, but more is needed. At this Baltic Breakfast, researchers from Stockholms universitets Östersjöcentrum present a selection of the most important measures marine researchers have identified for a healthier sea that can also support a sustainable blue economy.

content.title: The marine spatial plan sounds good, but does it apply to shipping?
content.description: Do the plans we write for the sea work in practice? Not quite, and not yet, according to new research. The ambitions are high. Sweden's marine spatial plan uses the right terminology: ecosystem approach, sustainability, coexistence. But what happens at sea paints a very different picture, for example when it comes to shipping.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden adopted its first marine spatial plan in 2022. The plan performs well in its language (the precautionary principle, integration, adaptation) but consistently fails at an operational level. Monitoring is neither binding nor cumulative. Sectors plan in silos and largely bypass marine spatial planning.
Sweden is also working towards a shift from road to sea, which is expected to increase maritime traffic by approximately 30% by 2029. Shipping is governed by international conventions (the International Maritime Organization, IMO) that Sweden cannot override, making the marine spatial plan's ecological commitments largely aspirational. The core problem is "institutional decoupling". Authorities and sectors adopt ecosystem language because it legitimises their plans, without actually changing their practices. Sustainability becomes a word in a document rather than a constraint on decisions.

content.title: How can bank data change and improve checks on companies?
content.description: Background checks are now crucial to securing business relationships and protecting society. As risks, money flows and business models evolve, however, established methods increasingly need current, context-sensitive perspectives to complement them.
content.extendedDescription:
Companies may look legitimate in registry data while actually being used for financial crime or unsound arrangements. Traditional background checks do not always detect warning signs in time, and when they do, it may already be too late.

At this seminar, Ekobrottsmyndigheten and Dun & Bradstreet describe how financial crime is evolving, what today's checks detect and what they miss. SRS Security then demonstrates how bank data and account analysis can complement traditional methods and improve decisions by revealing actual activity rather than registered information alone.

The panel also discusses tougher questions:
- Where is the line between legitimate risk analysis and excessive scrutiny?
- Which is more dangerous today: too little scrutiny or too much?
- What regulatory developments are needed to strengthen checks without compromising legal safeguards?

content.title: Can I swim? How do we secure knowledge of what is happening in the sea?
content.description: Effective environmental monitoring is essential for detecting changes in the environment that affect marine life, people along the coast and at sea, and businesses, in both the short and long term.
content.extendedDescription:
Those working in environmental monitoring currently need to cut the frequency of sampling, the number of samples and the types of samples taken. Several marine infrastructures – field stations, vessels and laboratories – essential for data collection and analysis face an uncertain future. This risks leaving many gaps in the picture we build, allowing changes in the marine environment to go undetected.

In this session, we want to:
• Explain why environmental monitoring matters.
• Give examples of when environmental monitoring has contributed to successful measures for a better marine environment.
• Discuss what needs to be done to safeguard existing time series and develop environmental monitoring for future challenges.

content.title: Can AI make regional development more accurately targeted?
content.description: Regional development often relies on statistics, analyses and forecasts based on historical data. Meanwhile, access to large datasets is growing rapidly. Can AI provide regions with better decision support and therefore more accurately targeted strategic priorities?
content.extendedDescription:
Regional development involves long-term decisions affecting labour markets, skills supply, innovation, infrastructure and business. These decisions rely heavily on statistics, analyses and forecasts describing past developments. Meanwhile, access to data is growing rapidly, from official statistics and authorities to mobility data, business data and other digital traces of societal development.
AI can analyse these datasets in new ways, providing more advanced forecasts and decision support. This raises a central question: can AI make regional development policy more data-driven and accurately targeted? Or does it risk reinforcing existing patterns and shifting the centre of decision-making from political judgements to algorithmic analysis?
How can AI be used in strategic regional development, and what opportunities and risks arise when data and advanced analysis play a greater role in how a region plans its future?

content.title: How can Sweden lead the way in the sustainable metal casting of the future?
content.description: Swedish industry faces a decisive question: how can we secure competitiveness, skills and sustainable production when the rest of the world is rapidly investing in next-generation manufacturing? Metal casting is a strategic but often invisible part of electrification, defence capability and the green transition.
content.extendedDescription:
Metal casting is a key technology for Swedish industry, from vehicles and energy to defence, electrification and advanced production. Meanwhile, international competition is intensifying. Countries that build strong testing and research environments and close cooperation with industry gain an advantage in innovation, skills provision and investment.
The seminar starts from the question of how Sweden can bring together industry, academia, research institutes and public organisations to shorten the path from research to industrial application. What is needed to make sustainable metal casting a Swedish strength? What investments, partnerships and political choices are required? And how can a regional industrial environment contribute to national competitiveness?
The discussion is not just about a new research centre, but about how Sweden can build the capability to stay at the forefront of next-generation sustainable manufacturing.

content.title: Medical research and innovation under pressure – can the next government meet voters' expectations?
content.description: A new geopolitical situation, increased preparedness efforts and growing threats to science make it harder to conduct critical activities such as life science research and development and quality-driven healthcare. How can the next government ensure Sweden does not fall behind?
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: Security and cooperation in the Baltic Sea – how can marine data strengthen defence and society?
content.description: Activities at sea generate large amounts of data that help to identify risks, protect infrastructure, and improve environmental monitoring. Data sharing raises questions about security, confidentiality, and governance. How can we strengthen security and cooperation among actors through data sharing?
content.extendedDescription:
The development of sensors, autonomous systems, and offshore infrastructure is generating large volumes of data collected by both public and private actors. These technologies often have dual-use applications and can support environmental and security-related monitoring as well as operational activities. In Sweden, however, this potential remains largely underutilized. One reason is that issues related to data access, ownership, and use remain unclear. At the same time, international experiences suggest that improved secure data sharing can create opportunities for collaboration between civilian and security stakeholders.

The seminar will be conducted in English and is organized within the framework of two research projects. Mistra Co-Creating Better Blue (C2B2), which explores how collaboration can strengthen ocean governance, and SAFEWIN, funded by Formas, which examines how dual-use technologies can contribute to secure data sharing and the protection of energy infrastructure.

content.title: How do we strengthen Sweden's medical preparedness in an era of crisis and war?
content.description: Sweden's security situation is changing, and demands on societal preparedness are growing. What role can medical research, education, collaboration and innovation play in strengthening the country's ability to handle future crises and conflicts? How can universities best contribute to medical preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
As geopolitical tensions rise and the focus on total defence grows, questions arise about how Sweden can strengthen its medical preparedness for future crises, disasters and ultimately war. What skills and resources are needed, and how can knowledge be put into practice more quickly? What role should medical research and education environments play in stronger total defence?

The discussion draws on Karolinska Institutet's strategic initiative on medical preparedness, bringing together research, education, innovation and cross-sector collaboration. It combines expertise in areas including health crises, disaster medicine, defence-related medicine and research into human performance and resilience in extreme environments.

The aim is to open up new perspectives and partnerships on one of the most pressing societal issues of our time. How should universities, public agencies, healthcare services and other societal actors work together to strengthen Sweden's ability to prevent, manage and learn from crises?

content.title: When systems crash – will digital preparedness hold up?
content.description: Attackers are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and digital preparedness must improve. By sharing information and experience, we can jointly strengthen our resistance and move from words to action to build resilient IT infrastructure that supports society.
content.extendedDescription:
In an increasingly uncertain world, threats to society's digital infrastructure are growing. Cyberattacks are becoming more advanced and increasingly target critical functions such as energy systems, transport, commerce and public services. The question is not whether, but when, systems will face serious disruption.
Meeting these threats requires more than technology. It requires collaboration, information sharing and the ability to turn insights rapidly into concrete action. Robust, resilient IT infrastructure is essential for society to function even during crises and in the grey zone between peace and war.
How can we strengthen digital preparedness in practice? What responsibility lies with business, the public sector and politicians, and how can we jointly increase resilience?
This panel brings together businesses, authorities, politicians and academia to discuss how Sweden can move from words to action and build digital infrastructure that holds up even when systems are put to the test.

content.description: The war in Ukraine has shown the world that energy is an instrument of power. When Russian missiles knocked out electricity and heating during winter, parliament went dark and millions were forced to live in darkness and freezing cold. How well equipped is Sweden's total defence to withstand a similar scenario?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has shown the world that energy is an instrument of power. When Russian missiles knocked out electricity and heating during winter, parliament went dark and millions were forced to live in darkness and freezing cold. How well equipped is Sweden's total defence to withstand a similar scenario? Russian cyberattacks on Poland's energy system show that we must be ready today.

How we protect critical infrastructure and ensure a robust energy supply is absolutely crucial to our preparedness in crisis and war. Without electricity, water and heating, all operations stop and the most vital functions in our homes cease to work. We bring together politicians, public-authority representatives and business leaders responsible for keeping Sweden's lights on, even when a crisis becomes reality. Resilience in the energy system is an important form of life insurance.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Cross-bloc cooperation or deadlock? The future of Swedish CCUS – carbon capture and storage
content.description: CCUS can give Sweden a new industrial future through carbon capture and storage – but policy is lagging behind. How do we build a national strategy and cross-bloc consensus that lasts, strengthens competitiveness and matches our neighbours' investments?
content.extendedDescription:
CCUS – carbon capture, utilisation and storage – has the potential to become both a new Swedish industry of the future and a crucial tool for achieving climate targets. Yet Sweden lacks a coherent national strategy and a long-term policy framework. In an unsettled world, investments risk being postponed if policy is perceived as short-sighted.
Several of our neighbours are now making substantial investments in carbon capture and storage, creating both competition and new opportunities for Nordic cooperation. For Sweden, this is about more than climate: it concerns industrial development, new value chains, exports and future jobs.

The seminar brings together politics and industry to discuss how broad, cross-bloc support for CCUS can be built and sustained across electoral terms. How do we create stable conditions for investment? What does it take to move from individual facilities to a new industry? And can Sweden take the next step from pioneer to a leading nation in carbon capture and storage?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: When crisis strikes – who keeps Sweden warm and the lights on?
content.description: With war in our neighbourhood, energy supply has become a security issue. Electricity and heat are essential for healthcare, industry and defence. content.extendedDescription: With war in our neighbourhood and growing geopolitical uncertainty, energy supply has become a central security policy issue. These are some of the questions we will discuss with representatives of industry, authorities and politics.

content.title: Neurodevelopmental conditions at school: risk, exclusion and the teacher who noticed
content.description: Pupils with neurodevelopmental conditions are more likely than others to be pushed out of school. Inadequate support and adjustments and poor wellbeing can have far-reaching consequences, placing many at risk of destructive behaviour. How can school promote health and offer a route out of risk for these young people?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from Attention's report ‘I was not easy to like’, offering insight into the daily lives of young people aged 10 to 16 with neurodevelopmental conditions who risk destructive behaviour and exclusion, their families and the professionals around them.

We explain why school can be both protective and risky, why digital environments can be both a lifeline and a danger, why leisure and belonging matter so much, and how relatives are often forced to shoulder an unreasonable burden.

Above all, Nicole, a young woman with personal experience of being at risk, shares examples of what truly makes a difference.

The seminar ends with a panel of politicians where Nicole holds the microphone and asks the questions she would have wanted answered when she was at risk.

content.title: How we can prevent more children from becoming perpetrators – and victims at the same time
content.description: Even at an early age, we can identify children at risk of being drawn into crime. Healthcare services often see them first, at child health centres, in school health services and in child psychiatry. But what do we do with that knowledge? Prevention is overshadowed in the debate about the age of criminal responsibility – how can early signals lead to early support?
content.extendedDescription:
Long before a child becomes involved in crime, they have often already been seen by healthcare services, at a child health centre, in school health services, dental care or child and adolescent psychiatry. We see the early signs: insecurity, school absence and symptoms without a medical explanation. Yet support too rarely arrives in time.

Even at an early age, we can identify children at risk of being drawn into crime. But what do we do with that knowledge? While the debate focuses on the age of criminal responsibility and incarceration, prevention receives less attention. How can we instead build a chain of early interventions, cooperation and follow-up before a child is recruited?

The child is both perpetrator and victim. The panel brings together a remand prison chaplain, a paediatrician, psychiatry and politics to discuss how healthcare, school health services and social services can jointly reverse the trend and recognise the child's needs in time.

content.title: Home births — from the child's perspective
content.description: There has been lively media debate about home births this year. Are they safe or not? Should they be publicly funded? What risks do home births pose to the child, and how can public funding be used to improve maternity care?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we will describe how emergency teamwork around the baby is crucial to survival without severe brain injury. We will explain what science says about the risks and benefits of home births, and why, from an ethical perspective, it may be questionable to allocate extra resources to healthy women expecting low-risk births if this reduces capacity to care for women with greater medical needs. Finally, we will present ways other than home births to develop maternity care so that women do not see giving birth at home as the safest option.

The seminar concludes with a panel debate involving invited decision-makers and representatives of medical professional associations.

content.title: Unequal gynaecological cancer care – who takes responsibility for equal access to testing and treatment?
content.description: Gynaecological cancer affects 3000 women and causes around 1200 deaths annually. This overlooked cancer group receives limited research resources and has modest survival rates. Waiting times for diagnosis and treatment are often long, access to molecular testing is unequal and few patients participate in clinical trials, hampering progress.
content.extendedDescription:
Gynaecological cancer includes cancer of the ovaries, endometrium, cervix or vulva, with ovarian and endometrial cancer being the most common. Early detection is crucial to improving survival, but little progress has been made in the past decade. Treatment is mainly surgical, with limited access to precision medicines, although development is accelerating.
Waiting times for diagnosis and treatment vary greatly between regions. The proportion of patients meeting the time targets in standardised care pathways (SVF) is far below the goal. Access to molecular testing and clinical trials is also uneven. Few are offered trial participation, with major regional differences. Inequality is exacerbated by a lack of organisation of care into appropriate levels in some regions, affecting access to specialised care and expertise. Developments in precision medicine place new demands on healthcare, requiring well-developed testing to analyse tumours' genetic characteristics. This is crucial to providing the right treatment to the right patient, regardless of where they live.
Lunch wraps are available.

content.title: Climate change and cultural heritage values
content.description: Climate change is accelerating risks of damage to cultural heritage. Extreme weather and temperature changes increase risks of moisture damage and physical deterioration. We need knowledge of how buildings with heritage value are affected by rapid climate change.
content.extendedDescription:
Climate change is increasingly evident in heritage environments through mould, rot and more insect attacks. Wall paintings are threatened by condensation damage, and masonry is fractured by more frequent swings between above- and below-freezing temperatures. Sweden still lacks strategic monitoring and thus systematic knowledge of the extent of damage. Norway has developed a method for climate monitoring of culturally significant buildings.

The seminar highlights known damage and discusses how agencies and heritage property managers could jointly build systematic knowledge to reduce and, ideally, prevent damage.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Migraine — an often overlooked condition affecting women: why do so few get the right treatment?
content.description: Migraine affects around 13 per cent of the population, mainly women of working age. Migraine-specific treatments exist, but requirements that only neurologists or headache specialists prescribe them create a bottleneck. The result is limited and unequal access for people with severe migraine.
content.extendedDescription:
Migraine is one of our major widespread diseases. For people with high-frequency migraine, targeted migraine-specific medicines have been developed for those with the greatest disease burden. Yet these treatments do not reach all severely affected patients.

Restricting prescribing to neurologists or headache specialists — a small specialist group responsible for a large patient population — creates bottlenecks and limited, unequal access. Patients whose condition is well managed and who could be referred back to primary care for follow-up occupy capacity, preventing or delaying access for those waiting for help.

How do we need to rethink our approach to ensure that innovations reach the right patients at the right time?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Democracy under threat? Is school fulfilling its societal mission?
content.description: Democracy can no longer be taken for granted, globally or here at home. When Swedish young people question its value and undemocratic forces gain ground, schools' democratic mission becomes more important than ever, particularly in an election year.
content.extendedDescription:
It is clear that we can no longer take democracy for granted, globally or here in Sweden. Challenges are visible not only in undemocratic trends internationally, but also in our immediate surroundings. Meanwhile, more Swedish young people, particularly young men, are questioning whether democracy really is the best form of government.

Schools have a crucial role in strengthening democracy and laying the foundations for the society of the future. But are they fulfilling their democratic mission, not only in classrooms but also in corridors where values are shaped every day? Are schools properly equipped, or do they need support from civil society? What responsibility do politicians have? And how does schools' work on democracy connect to total defence?

These are questions we will discuss during a seminar in Almedalen.

content.title: Renewing conservation
content.description: In the construction sector, conversion is beginning to challenge demolition and new construction as the norm. But both structural and formal barriers remain. Knowledge of the modern building stock's values, both as technical systems and as high-quality cultural environments, needs to be strengthened and shared.
content.extendedDescription: Most of the building stock was constructed after 1945. Re:purpose is a practice-oriented research project that has examined how office buildings from the late 1900s can be adapted and converted for new uses while retaining their cultural heritage value and architectural qualities. Three interdisciplinary teams have worked with three buildings. The project has resulted in proposals for policy changes that emphasise new ways of understanding value, improved environmental certification systems and the need for evidence based on a holistic approach and collaboration. At the seminar, we discuss, among other things, how building conservation needs to change to actively contribute to the careful stewardship of the modern building stock's values.

content.title: How do singing, music and culture contribute to resilience and democracy?
content.description: Art, literature, singing and music can challenge established world orders. They are a political force, another language in our turbulent world. They can support peaceful protest and healing. How does culture contribute to change and the shaping of a democratic society?
content.extendedDescription:
Tonight, we sing together about democracy, courage and hope, for the world's sake.
For centuries, culture has been used to stand up to injustice and abuses of power. Early this year, we saw a protest movement of songs spread across the United States as equal human worth was threatened by an indecent migration policy.
Tonight, we want to express "singing resistance". We sing for everyone worldwide who is forbidden to gather, silenced and denied opportunities for expression.
Culture is about resilience, survival and healing. It shapes our democratic society peacefully.
Music and stories protect not only our inner lives but also what risks being threatened: our language, history and identity.
In times of unrest and war, music is our strongest resource. It unites us in a collective peace movement across boundaries.
Let us sing tonight and raise the roof of Vårdklockans kyrka!

content.title: In remand custody: when can I see Mum again?
content.description: Behind the closed doors of remand centres are children longing for home, lost and vulnerable in society and in life. Perpetrators and victims at the same time. How do you answer their questions: when can I see Mum again? Why did everything go so wrong?
content.extendedDescription:
An evening of music and conversation about guilt, vulnerability, trust, responsibility, hopelessness and hope, but also the possibility of a new beginning.

What happens behind closed doors when a remand centre chaplain meets children longing for home? Children who have committed extremely serious crimes. Children terrified of death. Deeply distrustful of adults. Children whose ability to understand consequences is not fully developed. Children who are both perpetrators and victims.
Two things recur in these conversations: longing for Mum and the hardest question, why did everything go so wrong?
How can these children learn to find their boundaries again, for themselves and for others? What can help them discover their own ‘U-turn’, the thing that gives them a second chance? And what can we do when meeting children and young people?

Olle Jonasson is one of around 180 pastoral care workers, including pastors, priests, deacons and imams, working in remand centres and prisons across Sweden. Their work is coordinated by Sveriges kristna råd under an agreement with Kriminalvården.

content.title: Can measurement improve education, or do we risk measuring broader learning out of it?
content.description: Knowledge must be monitored and quality assured. But could a focus on what is measurable displace broader learning, judgement and democratic competence? How can governance encompass education's full purpose and nurture confident young people capable of action?
content.extendedDescription:
Monitoring and quality assurance are prerequisites for equitable schooling. But education is more than what appears in results. Broader learning, judgement and the ability to think independently and participate in a democratic society are equally crucial but harder to measure.

Swedish schooling has always oscillated between freedom and regulation, trust and control. The biggest school reforms in 30 years are now being implemented, with new curricula, a new grading system and increased regulation. The ambition matters. Meanwhile, the OECD highlights the importance of nurturing confident pupils who can navigate a complex world. How can we ensure that the entire mission, not just its measurable aspects, is present in encounters with children and pupils?

How can governance secure knowledge development without measuring broader learning out of education? How can we create security and trust? And what does quality in Swedish education really mean when we take the entire mission seriously in a time of climate transition and democratic retreat? These are the questions we explore.

content.title: From demolition to a new facade — how can reclaimed bricks become a large-scale industry?
content.description: The construction sector needs to reduce both climate impact and waste. Reusing building materials is often presented as a solution — but how can it work on a larger scale in practice? What systems are needed for collecting, quality-assuring and turning reclaimed materials into products?
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, reusing facing bricks has grown from a niche into a rapidly expanding part of the construction sector. Reclaimed facing bricks now account for more than ten per cent of Sweden's facing brick market.
The seminar describes how a large-scale reuse system can work in practice, from collecting bricks during demolition, through cleaning and quality assurance, to turning the material into CE-marked construction products.
We discuss the technical, logistical and regulatory conditions needed for reuse to work at scale, and how the industry can develop circular material flows in construction.
The seminar also addresses the ongoing expansion of production capacity in Sweden, where new investments, including support from Klimatklivet, enable more automated and efficient brick reuse facilities.

content.title: From preparedness plans to effective cooperation: building local robustness
content.description: Municipalities are strengthening civil preparedness, but how can ambitions translate into effective local cooperation? How do we build everyday robustness between municipalities, business and civil society?

How do we create structures in which the public sector, business and civil society work together before a crisis? How do we make community support points into active hubs? How do we build relationships that hold up under pressure? We help you succeed.

content.title: How great is the risk of China taking over?
content.description: Tensions between China and the United States are growing. Some say China is rising and the United States declining. Could China take over the world? How great is that risk? If it did, what would life in Sweden and Europe look like? Could the West stop China's advance?
content.extendedDescription:
China's global strategy is to start fires around the world so the United States cannot concentrate its strength on China. The United States does the opposite, trying to extinguish fires everywhere. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are part of the game. Persecution of dissenters within China also forms part of the CCP's global strategy to secure its domestic position while seeking world dominance. How would Swedish security, the economy and our democratic values be affected if the centre of gravity shifted eastwards?

Manyan Ng, one of Europe's leading China experts and an engaging speaker, shares his holistic, incisive and clear view of China. Manyan is a frequently consulted commentator for several media outlets. He accurately predicted developments in China's economy and global role over the past 20 years. For example, he predicted that China's economy would encounter many problems and that it was time to plan to protect investments there. A discussion of power and important strategic choices

content.title: What do we do when markets fail?
content.description: When market logic governs essential services, questions arise about accessibility, price and fairness. What happens when things people need — taxis, medicines, reliable trains or veterinary care — are shaped primarily by profitability rather than social responsibility?
content.extendedDescription:
What happens when market logic is applied to things people cannot do without — care for sick animals, taxis in rural areas, reliable trains, medicines or the ability to bury a loved one?
For several years, Tankesmedjan Tiden has examined markets where the promise of competition and choice has not been fully realised. Reports on veterinary care, taxis, vehicle inspections, pharmacies, railways and funerals reveal a common pattern: rising prices, growing urban–rural differences, poor accessibility and a system in which those most dependent on a service often have the least influence.
The seminar discusses the limits of markets. What happens when essential functions are governed primarily by profitability? How are ordinary people, working conditions and trust in society affected? And what political tools are needed when markets fail those who need them most?
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Politics and meaning after liberalism?
content.description: The era of liberalism is over and winds of change are blowing, but what comes next? What is the meaning of life, democracy's crisis and political renewal, and how do we include perspectives from different voices?
content.extendedDescription:
It was said that history had ended, liberal democracy had triumphed and the future promised continual improvement. That did not happen. Instead, we live amid intertwined economic, political and existential crises. How did we get here? And what can we do about it?

The panellists discuss the meaning of life, human nature and democracy's decline. How deep is our societal crisis, and how could politics have gone astray? What are the roles of the labour movement and LO? What would returning to its roots mean for social democracy? How does the centre-right view the weakening of liberalism?

Welcome to a discussion of political ideas based on Payam Moula's book Det goda, with panellists bringing different perspectives.

content.title: Advanced healthcare at home – an important provider making a difference
content.description: Advanced home healthcare has evolved from palliative care towards increasingly advanced treatment at home for several patient groups. content.extendedDescription:
The lecture describes how advanced home healthcare is organised, providing skilled care in patients' homes and access to its own inpatient services. Many enrolled patients have oncological or haematological diseases and undergo long-term treatment.

Multidisciplinary teams provide holistic care addressing medical and psychosocial needs. More people need to know the service exists and what it offers.

content.title: Electricity's Gordian knot: can the state unlock offshore wind investment?
content.description: Offshore wind can be expanded at industrial scale to meet growing electricity demand driven by industrial transition and more AI centres. Yet a gap separates industry's electricity price expectations from the cost of investing in new generation. How do we untie this Gordian knot?
content.extendedDescription:
Low electricity prices are essential to Swedish industry's electrification and competitiveness. Yet all new generation comes at a price that cannot be compared with old, fully depreciated generating assets.

The discrepancy between expectations of future electricity prices and conditions for investors in new generation is a Gordian knot that must be untied to accelerate electrification. Perhaps Sweden needs an electrification leap in which new production enables electricity use to expand? What might that look like? What roles must market actors play, and where must policymakers intervene?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: From bullied pupil to headteacher: what does life teach us about school?
content.description: Many pupils still experience bullying, racism and exclusion at school. How does this affect their lives, and what responsibility does school leadership have to break these patterns and create schools where every child has an equal chance to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Daria Ramzi has made an unusual journey, from a childhood marked by exclusion, racism and bullying to leading two schools and becoming a prominent voice on education, the fight against bullying and people's ability to change their lives.

In her book ‘Kan jag, så kan DU! Från förorten till makthavarlistan’, she speaks openly about experiences many recognise but that rarely feature in public debate. How does growing up feeling that you do not quite belong shape a person? What happens when adults respond to bullying and abuse with silence? What does it take to break patterns and create new possibilities?

We meet Daria Ramzi for a personal conversation about leadership, courage and identity. It moves between experiences of vulnerability and her role as a school leader today: fighting bullying at school and online, and hoping for schools where more children and young people can feel their future is possible.

content.title: Periods: no more taboos
content.description: It is time to talk more about periods. As long as menstruation remains taboo, it affects everything from girls' self-image to how decisions are made and resources allocated in society.
content.extendedDescription:
WaterAid and Lindex are hosting a menstrual health networking event to challenge stigma and highlight why knowledge is key to change.

Silence and stigma affect girls' self-esteem, education and opportunities to participate fully in society. How do we break taboos and make menstruation a natural part of conversations about gender equality, health and development?

During the evening, we share stories and examples of change when more people dare to take the issue seriously. What happens when knowledge spreads in schools, workplaces and politics? How can more people help break taboos?

Meet others who want change, have a drink and continue the conversation in Restaurang Vår Fru's beautiful courtyard in central Visby. It is an excellent opportunity to meet across sectors and put menstruation on the agenda. Clara Klingenström also joins the event to provide music.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: Menstrual health, empowerment and economic development
content.description: Menstruation is still surrounded by stigma, taboos and a lack of knowledge. When it is not treated as a societal issue, girls risk missing school and women being excluded from working life. Breaking taboos is about more than dignity and rights: it is about development, the economy and gender equality.
content.extendedDescription:
When girls can attend school and women can work, both household incomes and entire communities are strengthened. What happens to a society's productivity when girls and women are forced to be absent simply because they lack the means to manage their periods safely? How does access to water and toilets affect women's participation in the labour market? What responsibility do male decision-makers have to advance this issue?

The breakfast seminar focuses on why menstruation is still surrounded by stigma and its consequences for girls' education, women's labour-market opportunities and societies' economic development. We also discuss how investment in water, sanitation, knowledge and education can contribute to better menstrual health and more equal societies.
Together with participants from business and politics, we explore how menstruation can be elevated from a private concern to a question of rights, gender equality and sustainable development. What political changes are needed to increase investment?
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: From vision to reality – how do we make animal-free research the norm?
content.description: Increasing numbers of researchers, public agencies and societal actors express a desire to reduce and ultimately replace the use of animals in research. Yet millions of animals are still used globally in biomedical research every year.
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a panel debate bringing together researchers and other actors in the research system to discuss how to accelerate the transition to animal-free research methods. The discussion starts with how the vision of animal-free research can be put into practice and what is needed for animal-free methods to become the norm more widely.

The panel will highlight both opportunities and obstacles. Despite rapid development of new methods, such as advanced cell models, organ-on-chip technology and AI-based models, large numbers of laboratory animals are still used in research. Why is the transition so slow? Which structures in the research system need to change? And how can researchers, funders, public agencies and other actors work together to accelerate progress?

The panel will discuss research culture, funding, validation and implementation of new methods, and the role politics and society can play in driving change.

content.title: From income support to employment — how can the activity requirement make a real difference?
content.description: The activity requirement for income support could become a route to work — or an administrative dead end. What is needed for the reform to give people real steps towards employment, language skills, social connection and self-sufficiency?
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities will have major responsibility for offering activities that improve individuals' employment prospects. At the same time, many settings where people can develop, test their capacity for work and build networks are provided by nonprofit organisations, cooperative enterprises and other public-benefit employers.

What is needed for the activity requirement to ensure quality, employment protections and lasting results? And how can municipalities, Arbetsförmedlingen and nonprofit employers cooperate so that more people move from income support to empowerment and work?

Fremia invites you to a discussion about how the activity requirement must work in practice to strengthen individuals, the labour market and civil society's role. Fremia brings together politics, municipalities, civil society and employers to discuss implementation.

The event includes a presentation of Fremia's labour market report, focused entirely on the activity requirement for income support.

content.title: When children are victims of crime – how can their rights throughout the process be strengthened?
content.description: 57% of all children have experienced some form of violence. Yet society often fails to provide the right support in time. This makes child victims of crime one of our most vulnerable and overlooked groups. How can public agencies jointly create safer, more coherent systems for children affected by crime?
content.extendedDescription:
In Sweden, 57% of all children have experienced some form of violence while growing up. Society often fails to provide the right support in time. This makes child victims of crime one of our most vulnerable and also most overlooked groups. Yet public debate today tends to focus on gang crime and less on children who themselves experience crime.
Children exposed to violence encounter several parts of society – social services, police, prosecutors, healthcare and sometimes Barnahus centres. This seminar brings together Socialstyrelsen, Polismyndigheten, Åklagarmyndigheten and Barnafrid to discuss how children's rights can be strengthened throughout the process, from early detection, reporting and investigations to ongoing support.
Keeping the child at the centre, we highlight key challenges – such as parallel investigations, long waits, varying support measures and inadequate participation – and examine what these mean for the child.

content.title: How can we build an inclusive and safe local community in time?
content.description: Society's resilience takes shape in local communities. When children and young people have good conditions in which to grow up, people feel included and local stakeholders cooperate, both safety and confidence in the future are strengthened. How can we build inclusive communities over the long term that prevent exclusion and crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Many societal challenges develop over time. They are often preceded by a lack of hope for the future, poor school results, mental ill health or unsafe childhood environments. Long-term preventive work is therefore crucial.

Schools, civil society, municipalities, the police and business come together in local communities. When these actors cooperate, risks can be identified early and more children and young people can receive support to find their place in society.

A broader perspective on security is also needed. Financial stability, social cohesion and trust in society's institutions are important foundations for strengthening both inclusion and societal resilience.

Länsförsäkringar has a local presence throughout the country and sees every day how finances, health and security are connected in people's everyday lives. As an organisation with a key role in society, we want to contribute to a discussion about how long-term preventive work can strengthen inclusion, confidence in the future and security throughout Sweden.

content.title: Nordic gold at stake: trust and cohesion in today's Sweden
content.description: Sweden's high levels of trust, called "Nordic gold", have been crucial for cooperation, security and stable institutions. New research indicates declining trust in neighbours and major differences between areas. What happens when local trust erodes?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish society is characterised by high interpersonal trust and strong confidence in its institutions. We trust one another, authorities and the functioning of systems. This has created stability, security and long-term thinking. Yet there are signs that this picture is changing.
The seminar explores Gemenskapsbarometern, Sweden's largest population survey on trust, conducted jointly by LF Forskningsstiftelse and Institutet för bostads- och urbanforskning at Uppsala universitet.
As trust is challenged and social polarisation risks increasing, understanding what strengthens or weakens community in Sweden becomes ever more important. What does research say about these developments? Is Sweden still a high-trust country? Are there differences between neighbourhoods, regions and groups? What role do media and politics play in the development of trust and social cohesion?

content.title: When research meets the challenges facing schools
content.description: Schools must address societal challenges on a scientific basis. This is especially true today, as society and schools face one of their most complex periods in modern times, with digitalisation and AI changing how we learn and teach. Educational research is absolutely central here.
content.extendedDescription:
Digitalisation and AI bring both opportunities and challenges for teachers and pupils. Growing segregation creates schools with vastly different conditions, while increasing numbers of pupils face language challenges that require more than standard solutions. Educational research provides research-based knowledge for teachers and decision-makers at every level, including politicians.

Vetenskapsrådet works to ensure that research of the highest quality benefits all of society. At the seminar, research findings meet everyday school life. Researchers, teachers and decision-makers discuss the role of educational research in three of schools' most pressing challenges:
• How digitalisation and AI are changing the foundations of teaching and learning.
• How the consequences of segregation affect teachers' work.
• How challenges in children's and young people's reading and writing skills can be addressed.

content.title: What role does the financial sector play in future sustainability issues?
content.description: What role should banks, pension providers and insurers actually play in societal development, and which issues will shape the sustainability agenda ahead?
content.extendedDescription: Länsförsäkringar invites you to Almedalen's major sustainability round with Sweden's leading financial-sector sustainability executives. Geopolitical turmoil, AI as both enabler and threat, rising greenhouse gas emissions, growing climate adaptation needs, biodiversity loss, total defence development and the EU's Omnibus package simplifying sustainability rules shape the world around us. How do these affect financial actors' sustainability work? What issues are crucial to long-term business and societal benefits but may not even feature on management's agenda today? For 45 minutes, we discuss risks, opportunities and how finance can support positive development and future-proof society. Welcome to a duel featuring some of the country's most influential sustainability leaders.

content.title: Electronic tagging – an alternative to prison?
content.description: More and more people are sentenced to prison in Sweden while prisons become increasingly overcrowded. Could electronic tagging be a good alternative?
content.extendedDescription: More and more people are sentenced to prison in Sweden while prisons become increasingly overcrowded. At a time of tougher sentences, Swedish research shows that cost-effective alternatives can also reduce reoffending. At the seminar, you will hear current research findings, and a panel will discuss the opportunities and problems associated with potentially expanding electronic tagging.

content.title: Sustainable investment under pressure: how do we navigate the new rules?
content.description: Sustainable investment is under intense pressure as the security situation deteriorates and sustainability is dismissed as ‘woke’. Meanwhile, investors face difficult choices as geopolitical risks reshape the rules: should they stay invested and influence companies, or exclude them altogether?
content.extendedDescription:
In an increasingly conflict-ridden world, the defence and arms industries have become both more sought after and more debated. Many investors are reconsidering previous exclusions and opening up to defence investment, while others choose to reduce their exposure or entirely exclude countries such as the USA. At the same time, political initiatives, particularly in the USA, restrict consideration of ESG, diversity, equity and inclusion, and international climate commitments. This raises questions about the reliability of American companies and institutions when threats to leave shared frameworks actually materialise. Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an energy crisis. Could it reverse the trend and accelerate the transition?

The seminar focuses on how geopolitical risks should be managed in investment strategies and shareholder governance as pressure to address ESG decreases in some parts of the world but increases in others.

content.title: AI, You & I: When AI Thinks Like Us, Who Shapes Intelligence and Human Identity?
content.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of reasoning, creating and making decisions. As AI systems shape information, institutions and economies, this raises crucial questions about human identity, agency and who controls the intelligence influencing societies and global governance.
content.extendedDescription:
Artificial intelligence is evolving from a tool into a collaborator capable of generating knowledge, influencing decisions and shaping social systems. As AI becomes embedded in institutions, economies and everyday life, it challenges long-held assumptions about human identity, agency and control over knowledge.
Engaging India @ Almedalen brings together leaders from Sweden & India to explore global challenges through dialogue between policy, industry and academia. The 2026 series examines artificial intelligence through the lens of identity, industry and planetary transition.
This seminar explores how AI may redefine what it means to be human while also reshaping global power structures. Who shapes the intelligence that will influence societies, democratic institutions and international relations? And how can societies ensure that the development of AI reflects shared human values?

content.title: Gotland cannot wait – time to take long-term responsibility for the road across the sea
content.description: Gotland is part of Sweden, but access is determined by ferry services, which effectively function as the country's most expensive road. Prices affect residents, businesses and visitors. How can fair conditions and long-term access to and from Gotland be secured?
content.extendedDescription:
For Gotland, the ferry is not a supplement: it is Gotland's road and a prerequisite for equal living conditions. High ferry fares have direct consequences for businesses, residents and the public sector. And when Gotland's strategic importance to Sweden's preparedness and security has never been clearer, the issue goes beyond regional policy. A robust Sweden requires an accessible Gotland.

This seminar focuses on ferry fares to and from the island. They matter to all travellers, to transport and goods, and from a preparedness perspective. Access to Gotland matters to all of Sweden. The seminar is planned as a panel discussion on securing Gotland's accessibility now and in the future.

content.title: Stop wasting money on unnecessary reconstruction of outdoor spaces: think sustainably
content.description: We waste millions rebuilding parks and playgrounds that could have lasted for years if we had simply maintained them. Poor maintenance becomes a convenient excuse for expensive projects. Do we want to be sustainable, or just keep wearing out what we already have?
content.extendedDescription:
Reinvestment in parks and public spaces costs society millions, often unnecessarily. Inadequate care and maintenance accelerate deterioration, making expensive reconstruction the only solution. Good maintenance, the right materials and everyday attention could have prevented many of these projects.
Sustainable management is about more than repairs and tidying up. It gives places the opportunity to develop, retain their quality and age gracefully over time. It means recognising the value and potential of what already exists instead of allowing deterioration to continue and become an argument for building anew.
At a time of financial pressure and demanding sustainability requirements, the question is clear: why invest in reconstruction when millions can be saved by caring for what we already have? Sustainable environments require a long-term approach. Better management means less, and smarter, construction.

content.title: Swedish battery research – where are we heading?
content.description: Batteries are a key technology for portable electronics, but above all for our transport sector and future energy system. They are therefore absolutely essential to the industry, prosperity, resilience, security and climate ambitions of Sweden and the EU.
content.extendedDescription:
There are major challenges – geopolitical uncertainty and global competition – but also substantial initiatives to secure a European battery value chain. Sweden can play a relatively significant role within the EU and globally, given political prioritisation and even stronger cooperation between academia, industry and wider society.

The Swedish battery research and innovation roadmap being presented represents Sweden's ecosystem along the entire battery value chain. Its ultimate purpose is to strengthen Sweden's position and competitiveness in batteries through research, development and innovation.

We will present our overall vision as well as proposals for three concrete areas of action based on six key thematic areas of need. The roadmap has a national focus, but builds on the European “Battery 2030+ R&I Roadmap” to stimulate cooperation and collaboration with European partners as effectively as possible.

content.title: Smart policy for rapid nuclear power expansion
content.description: How can new policies accelerate construction and reduce the costs of new nuclear power to meet the current government's targets?
content.extendedDescription: While the parties supporting the current government have strongly supported new nuclear power, many in society, including other political parties, have reservations about costs, construction timelines and safety. Even with strong government support, considerable uncertainty remains about whether new nuclear power can be built in Sweden on time and on budget to meet the government's 2035 target of at least 2,500 megawatts of new nuclear capacity. Could better policy accelerate such expansion? This roundtable brings together policy experts to discuss and develop a broader range of policy options addressing nuclear power's challenges and opportunities for new construction that is affordable, sustainable, rapid and has genuine public support. We will draw on lessons from new Uppsala universitet research on nuclear construction in other countries, and from renewable energy projects in Sweden and abroad.

content.title: Knowledge and democracy under pressure – is the Swedish system holding up?
content.description: We live in a time when both knowledge and democracy face intense pressure worldwide. Politicians must make far-reaching decisions on climate, migration, crime and welfare, and need solid facts more than ever. But how well does Sweden's machinery for providing that knowledge work?
content.extendedDescription:
We read about legislation passed despite warnings from consultation bodies, experts and Lagrådet. What happens if confidence in the process begins to falter and decision-makers start distrusting public administration and experts generally?
New research shows that broad, independent committee inquiries have gradually been replaced by rapid, politically directed inquiries with narrow terms of reference, short deadlines and predetermined directions. The evidence base becomes thinner and independence weaker. The result is poorer laws, poorer decisions and ultimately eroded trust in both democracy and scientific experts, just when polarisation is at its worst. So what is needed to equip the system for the future, and who takes the lead: government, parliament, public authorities, researchers or civil society? What does it take for our democratic rules to endure in an ever faster-moving world? Are new institutional solutions needed, and if so, what would they look like?

content.title: When customers click for sustainability – can we deliver nationwide?
content.description: More people want fossil-free deliveries, but the transition is fastest in major cities and along profitable routes. Sustainable deliveries risk becoming a big-city privilege. How can we make the transition work nationwide without compromising service, price or accessibility?
content.extendedDescription:
E-commerce and growing home delivery make transport increasingly visible to customers. Meanwhile, proposals are being discussed to scrap the target of cutting transport-sector emissions by 70 per cent by 2030 and introduce an electrification target instead. This puts even greater focus on what is actually feasible nationwide.

Conditions differ radically between urban and sparsely populated areas, and between high-volume flows and rural routes. If sustainable deliveries work only where volumes are large and alternatives plentiful, we risk a two-tier transition.

The seminar examines everyday conditions facing fuel suppliers, logistics operators and retailers with customers nationwide. We discuss what requirements, customer promises and collaboration models can actually be met, how checkout choices and communication influence demand, and what is needed to scale up more sustainable fuels. How can we design rules and business arrangements that make sustainable deliveries the norm rather than an optional extra?

content.title: Rail's role in jobs, climate and preparedness
content.description: A functioning, modern railway is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness. Investment in Swedish rail can create tens of thousands of jobs, reduce emissions and strengthen preparedness. How do we move from today's small, short-term solutions to the major investments that are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Unionen wants substantial long-term investments that improve accessibility for both people and freight and build on rail's historically important role in Swedish welfare. Today's investments create tomorrow's jobs and a more competitive Sweden.

The discussion focuses on national priorities needed for more and better jobs, greater transport capacity and a safe, secure labour market.

Welcome to an open, solutions-focused panel discussion about a future-proof railway policy and the investments needed today, tomorrow and beyond.

content.title: Physiological optimisation – how does the human body cope with war?
content.description: How do we strengthen human capabilities in extreme, high-risk environments? Cold, sleep deprivation and stress strain the body and mind. With the right knowledge, we can reduce injuries, strengthen resilience and create sustainable operational capability without compromising long-term health or the return to civilian life.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar brings together perspectives from research, defence and industry to examine human capabilities and vulnerabilities in war and serious crises. How are performance, decision-making and recovery affected when people operate in environments involving extreme cold, heavy physical demands, infection risks, advanced technical systems and repeated traumatic events?
The discussion takes a holistic view of the human dimension, from physiological and cognitive limitations to immune function and mental health over time. Particular attention is given to prevention and support for PTSD and increased suicide risk following deployment.

The seminar highlights how knowledge can be applied in practice: in requirements profiles, training, equipment and operational approaches, as well as long-term support before, during and after service. A central question is how responsibility can be shared between the state, employers and business to ensure that people working in extreme environments receive appropriate protection, support and follow-up.

content.title: Evictions affecting children are increasing – what can we do?
content.description: Despite the zero vision, evictions of families with children are increasing. Between January and June 2025, 422 children were affected by evictions, an increase of almost 60 per cent in three years. Why is it so hard to stop evictions affecting children?
content.extendedDescription: At the seminar, Frälsningsarmén highlights the conflict between the Convention on the Rights of the Child and tenancy law, geographical differences and the groups most affected. At least 5,900 children today live in homelessness with a parent, often a woman who has fled violence. Frälsningsarmén has therefore launched the Housing First project Hedvig, aimed at women and children exposed to violence. But what are politicians doing? Panel discussion.

content.title: Sweden: a stain on the Nordic region's reputation?
content.description: Sweden ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2008. Yet consistent findings from UN reviews, civil society and research show that the Convention's rights are not being satisfactorily implemented in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
We see human rights being weakened around the world. The threat to the rule of law in Sweden is highly topical, with lawyers issuing public appeals. Amid all this, two of our neighbours, Iceland and Norway, decided as recently as December 2025 to strengthen the status of disability rights by incorporating the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities into national law. Finland enacted legislation when it ratified the Convention. There are further examples in Europe, such as Spain, where the Convention has been strengthened through a constitutional amendment.

Join a discussion on the state of human rights in Sweden, focusing on the status of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Why is Sweden falling behind its neighbours when it comes to making the Convention Swedish law?

The seminar is organised as part of Civilsamhällesarenan.
